items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone may substitute, both men and women, but clarifies that a person is not permitted to substitute; if one does substitute, it is effective and he receives lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone may substitute, both men and women, but clarifies that a person is not permitted to substitute; if one does substitute, it is effective and he receives lashes.

items.text: Gemara's initial contradiction and scriptural challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's initial contradiction and scriptural challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction: the Mishnah first says 'everyone may substitute' (permissively), then says 'not that a person is permitted to substitute' (prohibitively). It then notes that the same difficulty arises from the verse 'He shall not exchange it nor substitute it,' which implies prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the mishna: it first says 'everyone substitutes' (implying ab initio) and then says 'not that a person is permitted' (implying only after the fact).
The Gemara objects that if the mishna meant ab initio, the verse 'He shall not substitute it' would contradict it, so the mishna must be understood differently.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reinterprets the Mishnah: it means 'everyone may effect substitution' (i.e., the substituted animal becomes holy), not that one is permitted to substitute; if one does substitute, it is effective and he receives lashes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reinterprets the Mishnah: it means 'everyone may effect substitution' (i.e., the substituted animal becomes holy), not that one is permitted to substitute; if one does substitute, it is effective and he receives lashes.

items.text: Inclusion of an heir
items.text_en: Inclusion of an heir
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'everyone' includes, and answers: an heir, and this is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda (who holds an heir cannot substitute).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the comprehensive term 'everyone' serves to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes an heir, and this mishna is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on heir's ability to substitute and lay hands
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on heir's ability to substitute and lay hands
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Meir holds an heir may lay hands and substitute; Rabbi Yehuda holds an heir may not. The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning by deriving the beginning of consecration from the end of consecration, and then analyzes the scriptural sources for laying hands and substitution, including alternative interpretations for the verses.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the dispute: Rabbi Meir says an heir may lay hands and substitute; Rabbi Yehuda says an heir may not.
The Gemara asks for Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and explains that he derives the beginning of consecration from the end of consecration.
The Gemara asks the source for the halakha of placing hands and answers that three instances of 'his offering' exclude a gentile, another's offering, and a father's offering (inheritor).
The Gemara objects: according to Rabbi Meir, how does he interpret the third 'his offering'? It answers that he uses it to include joint owners in the requirement of placing hands.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda does not accept joint owners for placing hands, or alternatively, he derives gentile and another's offering from one verse, leaving one verse for joint owners.
The Gemara asks for Rabbi Meir's reasoning that an heir can substitute, and answers that the verse 'if he shall at all substitute' includes the inheritor.

items.text: Derivation of supporting hand on substitute from initial dedication
items.text_en: Derivation of supporting hand on substitute from initial dedication
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that just as one may support a hand on the initial dedication, so too one may support a hand on the substitute offering, based on a verbal analogy between the end of dedication and the beginning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the beginning of dedication to the end, teaching that just as one may support a hand on the initial dedication, so too one may support a hand on the substitute offering.

items.text: Inclusion of women in temurah
items.text_en: Inclusion of women in temurah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda uses the extra phrase 'וְאִם הָמֵר יָמִיר' to include women in the law of temurah, while Rabbi Meir derives it from the word 'וְאִם'. The Gemara then explains why a separate verse is needed despite the general principle that women are equal to men for all punishments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with the extra phrase 'וְאִם הָמֵר יָמִיר'.
The Gemara answers that the phrase comes to include women in the law of temurah, citing a baraita that derives this from the verse.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir derives the inclusion of women.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Meir derives it from the word 'וְאִם', while Rabbi Yehuda does not expound that word.

The Gemara objects that without the verse, one might think a woman who performs temurah is not liable, citing Rav Yehuda and the school of Rabbi Yishmael that the Torah equates women to men for all punishments.

The Gemara resolves that a separate verse is needed because the punishment for temurah is not universal (the public and partners cannot perform temurah), so without the verse one might exempt women; the verse teaches otherwise.

items.text: Can a minor effect temurah?
items.text_en: Can a minor effect temurah?
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama raises the question of whether a minor who has reached the age of vows can effect temurah. The Gemara considers whether, since such a minor's dedications are valid, his temurah might also be valid, or whether the fact that he is not subject to punishments prevents temurah from taking effect.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a minor can effect temurah, and clarifies that the question applies only to a minor who has reached the age of vows, since one who has not cannot even dedicate.

The Gemara presents the two sides of the dilemma: since such a minor's dedications are valid, perhaps his temurah is also valid, or perhaps because he is not subject to punishments, temurah does not take effect.

items.text: Can a gentile effect temurah?
items.text_en: Can a gentile effect temurah?
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama then asks whether a gentile can effect temurah. The Gemara cites a baraita stating that gentiles' consecrated animals do not effect temurah, but Rami bar Chama's question is limited to a case where a gentile dedicates an animal for atonement of a Jew.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama raises a dilemma: if a minor can effect temurah, can a gentile do so, given that gentiles can consecrate animals but are not subject to punishments?
Rava cites a baraita stating that gentiles' consecrated animals do not effect temurah, implying that a gentile cannot perform substitution.
Rabbi Yosi adds a stringency regarding Temple maintenance but the baraita still concludes that gentiles do not effect temurah.

items.text: Gentile dedicates for atonement of a Jew
items.text_en: Gentile dedicates for atonement of a Jew
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama specifies his question: when a gentile dedicates an animal for the atonement of a Jew, do we follow the dedicator (gentile) or the one being atoned (Jew)? The Gemara attempts to resolve this from a statement of Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama specifies his question: when a gentile dedicates an animal for the atonement of a Jew, do we follow the dedicator (gentile) or the one being atoned (Jew)?

sub.text: Stam (suggesting a resolution from Rabbi Avahu)
sub.text_en: Stam (suggesting a resolution from Rabbi Avahu)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to resolve the dilemma from a statement of Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan, which distinguishes between the one who consecrates (adds one-fifth) and the one who achieves atonement (effects substitution).

items.text: Clarification of the previous sugya regarding temurah
items.text_en: Clarification of the previous sugya regarding temurah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies a previous point about the benefit of temurah for another person, distinguishing between cases where the offering comes through a Jew and where it does not. It concludes with a question about whether the entire process must be in the domain of the one making the temurah, left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the previous sugya: if one makes temurah on another's offering, the benefit of the exchange belongs to the other person, so how can the temurah be valid?

The Gemara answers that there the offering comes through the power of a Jew, so we follow the one who achieves atonement, but here the question remains whether the entire process must be in the domain of the one making temurah, and it is left unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Gentile offerings: no benefit, no me'ilah, no piggul, notar, or tum'ah
items.text_en: Gentile offerings: no benefit, no me'ilah, no piggul, notar, or tum'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that gentile offerings are forbidden for benefit by rabbinic law, but not subject to me'ilah by Torah law, derived from a gezeirah shavah from terumah. Similarly, they are exempt from piggul, notar, and tum'ah, derived through scriptural analogies involving the phrase 'Bnei Yisrael'.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that gentile offerings are forbidden for benefit by rabbinic law and exempt from me'ilah by Torah law.
The Gemara derives the exemption from me'ilah via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'חטא' from תרומה (terumah), where the verse specifies 'בני ישראל' excluding gentiles.
The Gemara cites the verse regarding טומאה (ritual impurity) that specifies 'בני ישראל', excluding gentiles from liability for piggul, notar, and tum'ah.
The Gemara derives the exemption for notar via a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) of 'חילול' from tum'ah, where the verse excludes gentiles.
The Gemara derives the exemption for piggul via a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) of 'עון' from notar, concluding that all these laws apply only to 'בני ישראל' and not to gentiles.

items.text: Gentiles cannot perform temurah
items.text_en: Gentiles cannot perform temurah
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides two reasons why gentiles cannot perform temurah: one from a verse linking temurah to Bnei Yisrael, and another from a chain of analogies connecting temurah to ma'aser behemah and ma'aser dagan, which explicitly excludes gentiles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'לֹא יַחֲלִיפֶנּוּ וְלֹא יָמִיר' (he shall not exchange it nor substitute it) and notes that the context begins with 'דַּבֵּר אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' (speak to the children of Israel), thereby excluding gentiles from the law of temurah.

The Gemara offers an alternative derivation: temurah of an animal is linked (הוקש) to ma'aser behemah (animal tithe), which is linked to ma'aser dagan (grain tithe), and regarding grain tithe the verse states 'בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' (children of Israel), excluding gentiles.

items.text: Gentile offerings: nesachim and me'ilah in kodshei bedek habayit
items.text_en: Gentile offerings: nesachim and me'ilah in kodshei bedek habayit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon rules that a gentile does not bring nesachim, but his offering requires them, derived from the verse 'ezrach'. Rabbi Yosei is stringent regarding all these matters. The Gemara distinguishes between kodshei mizbe'ach, where me'ilah does not apply to gentile offerings, and kodshei bedek habayit, where it does, because the gezeirah shavah applies only to items with inherent sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that Rabbi Shimon rules a gentile does not bring nesachim (libations) but his offering requires them, derived from the verse 'אזרח' (citizen) and 'ככה' (thus).
Rabbi Yosei states he is inclined to be stringent regarding all these matters because the word 'לה׳' (to the Lord) is written in the relevant verse.

The Gemara explains that the exemption from me'ilah (misappropriation) applies only to kodshei mizbe'ach (offerings with inherent sanctity), but for kodshei bedek habayit (temple maintenance funds with monetary sanctity), me'ilah does apply, because the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from terumah is limited to items with inherent sanctity.

items.text: General principle: negative commandment without action is exempt, with exception of temurah
items.text_en: General principle: negative commandment without action is exempt, with exception of temurah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav states that for any negative commandment, if one performs an action, he is liable; if not, he is exempt. The Gemara objects from temurah, which is a negative commandment without action yet carries lashes. Rav responds that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yehudah, who holds that one is liable even without action. The Gemara then questions this because the beginning of the mishnah includes an heir, which contradicts Rabbi Yehudah's view. It resolves that this Tanna agrees with Rabbi Yehudah on one point (lashes for inaction) but disagrees on another (heir can perform temurah).

sub.text: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav states a general principle: for any negative commandment, if one performs an action, he is liable; if not, he is exempt.

The Gemara objects: is it a general rule that a negative commandment without action is exempt? Temurah (המרה) is a negative commandment without action, yet one receives lashes, as taught in the mishnah.
Rav responds that the mishnah follows Rabbi Yehudah, who holds that one is liable (לוקין) even for a negative commandment without action.

The Gemara questions: can you really establish the mishnah as Rabbi Yehudah? The beginning of the mishnah includes an heir (יורש) in the rule 'everyone may perform temurah', which contradicts Rabbi Yehudah's view.

The Gemara resolves that this Tanna agrees with Rabbi Yehudah on one point (lashes for inaction) but disagrees on another: Rabbi Yehudah holds that an heir does not perform temurah, while this Tanna holds that an heir does perform temurah.

items.text: Exceptions to the principle: shevu'ah, temurah, and others
items.text_en: Exceptions to the principle: shevu'ah, temurah, and others
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili lists exceptions to the rule: one who swears falsely, one who performs temurah, and one who curses another with God's name are liable even without action. Another version adds one who separates terumah before bikurim. The Gemara begins to derive the source for the exception of shevu'ah from a verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili states the general rule that for any negative commandment, action triggers liability and inaction exempts, except for swearing falsely, performing temurah, and cursing another with God's name.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds another exception: one who separates תרומה (priestly portion) before ביכורים (first fruits) is also liable without action.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the exception for one who swears falsely?

Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Meir answers by citing the verse 'כִּי לֹא יְנַקֶּה ה׳ אֵת אֲשֶׁר יִשָּׂא אֶת שְׁמוֹ לַשָּׁוְא' (for the Lord will not acquit one who takes His name in vain), implying liability by the heavenly court even without action.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase 'but the earthly court lashes and cleanses him'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase 'but the earthly court lashes and cleanses him'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye why the verse says 'the Lord will not cleanse him' implying that the earthly court does cleanse him. Abaye explains that the extra word 'Lord' teaches that only the heavenly court does not cleanse, but the earthly court lashes and cleanses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye why the Mishnah's phrase implies that the earthly court cleanses, suggesting instead that the verse should mean no cleansing at all.
Abaye explains that the extra word 'Lord' in the verse teaches that only the heavenly court does not cleanse, but the earthly court lashes and cleanses him.

items.text: Derivation of lashes for a false oath from a vain oath
items.text_en: Derivation of lashes for a false oath from a vain oath
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives that a false oath (shevuat sheker) also incurs lashes from the double occurrence of 'lashav' in the Torah, applying the principle that if a verse is not needed for one case, apply it to another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the source for a vain oath (שבועת שוא), but from where do we derive lashes for a false oath (שבועת שקר)?
Rabbi Yochanan derives that the double occurrence of 'לשוא' (in vain) in the verse teaches that if it does not apply to a vain oath, apply it to a false oath, for which one is lashed.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's challenge: What is a false oath?
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's challenge: What is a false oath?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu questions the definition of a false oath. If it is 'I will not eat' and he ate, that involves an action. If it is 'I will eat' and he did not eat, there is a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish whether one is lashed for a negative commandment without action or for a doubtful warning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu objects: what is a false oath? If one says 'I will not eat' and then eats, that involves an action; if one says 'I will eat' and does not eat, is he lashed? It was stated that Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish say he is not lashed.
Rabbi Yochanan says he is not lashed because it is a negative commandment without an action (לאו שאין בו מעשה), and for such a negative commandment one is not lashed.
Resh Lakish says he is not lashed because it is a warning of uncertainty (התראת ספק), and for such a warning one is not lashed.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's resolution: False oath about the past
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's resolution: False oath about the past
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu proposes that the false oath is about the past, e.g., 'I ate' or 'I did not eat'. Rava explains that the Torah explicitly equates a false oath (sheker) to a vain oath (shav): just as a vain oath is about the past, so too a false oath is about the past.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu resolves the problem by proposing that the false oath (שבועת שקר) which incurs lashes is about the past, e.g., 'I ate' or 'I did not eat'.
Rava explains that the Torah explicitly equates a false oath (שקר) to a vain oath (שוא): just as a vain oath is about the past, so too a false oath is about the past.

items.text: Objection from a Mishnah and resolution: Rabbi Yishmael's view
items.text_en: Objection from a Mishnah and resolution: Rabbi Yishmael's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects from a Mishnah that implies only future oaths incur a sacrifice, excluding past oaths from lashes. The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who exempts past oaths from a sacrifice but still holds that one is lashed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects to Rabbi Avahu by citing a Mishnah that implies only future oaths incur a sacrifice, excluding past oaths from lashes.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who exempts past oaths from a sacrifice but still holds that one is lashed.

items.text: Second objection from the same Mishnah and resolution: Rabbi Akiva's view
items.text_en: Second objection from the same Mishnah and resolution: Rabbi Akiva's view
items.desc_en: Another objection from the Mishnah's second clause suggests that past oaths are exempt from lashes. The Gemara answers that this clause follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that a sacrifice is brought for past oaths, but lashes are still possible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah's second clause: the word 'זוֹהִי' (this is) excludes 'אכלתי ולא אכלתי' (I ate and I did not eat) from lashes.
The Gemara answers that the exclusion is only from a sacrifice, not from lashes, and this clause follows Rabbi Akiva who holds that a sacrifice is brought for past oaths.

items.text: Reconciliation: Both clauses follow Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Reconciliation: Both clauses follow Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes the inconsistency of attributing the first clause to Rabbi Yishmael and the second to Rabbi Akiva, and instead concludes both clauses follow Rabbi Akiva. The first clause excludes future oaths (like 'I will eat' and did not eat) from a sacrifice, not past oaths from lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the first clause was attributed to Rabbi Yishmael, but since the second clause follows Rabbi Akiva, the first must also follow Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara resolves that the first clause does not exclude past oaths from lashes, but rather excludes future oaths (like 'I will eat' and did not eat) from a sacrifice.

items.text: Interlude: The Tanna should not teach 'umeimer'
items.text_en: Interlude: The Tanna should not teach 'umeimer'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan instructs the Tanna not to teach the word 'umeimer' (and saying) because speech itself constitutes an action in the context of oaths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara digresses: regarding 'umeimer' (and saying), Rabbi Yochanan told the Tanna not to teach it, because with his speech he performed an action (and thus it is a negative commandment with an action).

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's instruction to the Tanna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's instruction to the Tanna
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan instructs the Tanna not to teach 'וּמֵימֵר' because speech itself constitutes an action in the context of oaths.

items.text: Source for lashes for cursing a fellow in God's name
items.text_en: Source for lashes for cursing a fellow in God's name
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya derives lashes for cursing a fellow in God's name from the verse 'if you do not observe' and 'the Lord will make your plagues extraordinary'. The Gemara then distinguishes this from a vain oath and from swearing to fulfill mitzvot, concluding that cursing a fellow involves two transgressions (vain oath and causing pain) yet still incurs lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one who curses a fellow in God's name receives lashes.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya derives lashes from the verse 'if you do not observe' and 'the Lord will make your plagues extraordinary', interpreting 'extraordinary' as lashes via the verse 'and the judge shall cast him down and strike him'.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the verse applies even to a true oath, not just cursing.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that a true oath is explicitly permitted by the verse 'the oath of the Lord shall be between them'.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the verse only permits swearing to appease a fellow, but does not exempt from lashes for cursing.
The Gemara rejects the objection, citing the verse 'and in His name you shall swear' which permits swearing in God's name generally.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'and in His name you shall swear' is needed for Rav's teaching that one may swear to fulfill mitzvot, citing 'I have sworn and I will keep Your righteous judgments'.
The Gemara concludes that the verse 'and in His name you shall swear' comes to teach about one who curses a fellow in God's name.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the verse applies to one who utters God's name in vain, not specifically to cursing a fellow.
The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that cursing a fellow in God's name is no less severe than uttering God's name in vain.

The Gemara reframes the objection: perhaps uttering God's name in vain alone suffices for lashes, but cursing a fellow involves two transgressions (vain utterance and causing pain) and might not incur lashes.
The Gemara resolves that despite the two transgressions, one who curses a fellow in God's name still incurs lashes.

items.text: Gemara's question about the source for the prohibition of uttering God's name in vain
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the source for the prohibition of uttering God's name in vain
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source for the prohibition of uttering God's name in vain, suggesting it might be derived from 'You shall not curse the deaf'. It then considers that this verse might only apply to cursing a fellow, and asks where the warning for uttering God's name in vain comes from. The response cites 'You shall fear the Lord your God and Him you shall serve', but this is identified as a positive commandment, not a prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source for the prohibition of uttering God's name in vain, considering whether it might be derived from 'You shall not curse the deaf', and then asks where the warning for uttering God's name in vain comes from.
The Gemara suggests that the source might be 'You shall fear the Lord your God and Him you shall serve', but then identifies this as a positive commandment (אזהרת עשה), not a prohibition.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement about one who presents terumah before first fruits
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement about one who presents terumah before first fruits
items.desc_en: In the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina, it is said that one who presents terumah before first fruits also violates a prohibition. The Gemara explains the reasoning: the verse 'Your fullness and your drip do not delay' refers to first fruits as 'fullness' and terumah as 'drip', and the command 'do not delay' prohibits delaying terumah after first fruits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina that one who presents terumah before first fruits also violates a prohibition.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement.

The Gemara explains the reasoning: the verse 'Your fullness and your drip do not delay' identifies first fruits as 'fullness' and terumah as 'drip', and the command 'do not delay' prohibits delaying terumah after first fruits.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina on lashes
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina on lashes
items.desc_en: It was stated: If one presented terumah before first fruits, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina disagree. One says he is lashed, the other says he is not lashed. The Gemara attempts to conclude that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina is the one who says he is lashed, based on his earlier statement that one who presents terumah before first fruits is lashed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina regarding whether one who presents תרומה (priestly portion) before ביכורים (first fruits) is lashed.

The Gemara attempts to conclude that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina is the one who says he is lashed, based on his earlier statement that one who presents תרומה (priestly portion) before ביכורים (first fruits) is lashed.

items.text: Alternative conclusion from a Mishnah that Rabbi Elazar says lashes
items.text_en: Alternative conclusion from a Mishnah that Rabbi Elazar says lashes
items.desc_en: The Gemara counters that perhaps Rabbi Elazar is the one who says lashes, citing a Mishnah about two baskets of tevel where one declares the tithe of one basket to be in the other. The Gemara then states that it was said: Rabbi Elazar says he is lashed because he presented second tithe before first tithe. The Gemara concludes that this is conclusive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara counters that perhaps Rabbi Elazar is the one who says lashes, citing a Mishnah about two baskets of tevel where one declares the tithe of one basket to be in the other.
The Mishnah continues with the case of declaring the tithe of each basket in the other, and the case of declaring the tithes of both baskets in each other, where one must invoke the Name.
The Gemara states that it was said: Rabbi Elazar says he is lashed because he presented second tithe before first tithe, and concludes that this is conclusive.

items.text: Difficulty with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's position
items.text_en: Difficulty with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: If Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina says he is not lashed, then there is a contradiction between his earlier statement (that one who presents terumah before first fruits is lashed) and this new position. The Gemara begins to resolve this, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina says he is not lashed, then there is a contradiction between his earlier statement (that one who presents terumah before first fruits is lashed) and this new position.
The Gemara begins to resolve the contradiction, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's question on premature terumah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on premature terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one who separates terumah before bikkurim is not lashed, given that the prohibition involves speech (a deed), similar to temurah which is punishable by lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by explaining that the earlier statement refers to a prohibition without action, for which one is not lashed, and cites Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's addition regarding one who separates תרומה (priestly portion) before ביכורים (first fruits).

The Gemara asks why temurah (substitution) is punishable by lashes because it involves a deed through speech, while one who separates תרומה before ביכורים should similarly be lashed for the same reason.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's answer: a לאו שניתק לעשה
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's answer: a לאו שניתק לעשה
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin answers that the prohibition of premature terumah is a לאו שניתק לעשה (a negative commandment that can be rectified by a positive one), based on the verse 'from all your tithes you shall separate', so lashes are not given.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin answers that the prohibition of premature terumah is a לאו שניתק לעשה (a negative commandment rectified by a positive one), citing the verse 'from all your tithes you shall separate'.

items.text: Abaye's objection from temurah
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from temurah
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that temurah itself is a לאו שניתק לעשה, yet the Mishnah states that one who makes temurah is lashed, contradicting Rabbi Avin's principle.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Dimi's teaching by asking whether every לאו שניתק לעשה (prohibition coupled with a positive commandment) is exempt from lashes.
Abaye objects that temurah (תמורה) is a לאו שניתק לעשה, yet the Mishnah rules that one who makes temurah is lashed, contradicting the principle that such prohibitions carry no lashes.

items.text: Resolution: two negatives and one positive
items.text_en: Resolution: two negatives and one positive
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that temurah involves two negative commandments and one positive, so the positive cannot override both negatives, hence lashes apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that temurah involves two negative commandments and one positive, so the positive cannot override both negatives, hence lashes apply.

items.text: Counterexample of an אונס (coerced divorce)
items.text_en: Counterexample of an אונס (coerced divorce)
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the case of an אונס (one who raped a woman and then divorced her), which has one negative and one positive, yet a priest who does so is lashed, contradicting the principle. The Gemara deflects by noting that priests have additional sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the case of an אונס (coerced divorce) as a counterexample: it has one negative and one positive commandment, yet a priest who does so is lashed, contradicting the principle that a positive commandment cannot uproot a negative one.
The Gemara deflects the counterexample by noting that priests have additional sanctity (קדושה יתירא), so the case of a priest is a separate reason and does not challenge the general principle.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on לאו שניתק לעשה
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on לאו שניתק לעשה
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yaakov regarding the leftover of the Paschal lamb: Rabbi Yehuda holds that a לאו שניתק לעשה is punishable by lashes, while Rabbi Yaakov holds that it is not, attributing the exemption to it being a לאו שאין בו מעשה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the verse 'לֹא יַשְׁאִירוּ מִמֶּנּוּ עַד בֹּקֶר' (they shall not leave any of it until morning) gives an עשה (positive commandment) after a לא תעשה (prohibition), teaching that one is not lashed for violating it.

Rabbi Yaakov objects that the exemption is not due to the עשה (positive commandment) but because it is a לאו שאין בו מעשה (a prohibition without an action), and such prohibitions are not punishable by lashes.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yaakov's statement that Rabbi Yehuda holds that one is lashed for violating this prohibition.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse for burning leftovers
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse for burning leftovers
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yaakov uses the verse 'the leftover shall be burned in fire' to teach that the burning can be done on the second morning (16th of Nisan), not for the positive commandment. This is supported by a baraita and Hezekiah's teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose the verse 'the leftover shall be burned in fire' serves for Rabbi Yaakov, who does not use it for the positive commandment.

The Gemara explains that the verse is needed for the baraita teaching that leftover sacrificial meat and bones are burned on the sixteenth of Nisan, and if that falls on Shabbat, they are burned on the seventeenth.
Hezekiah and the Tanna of the school of Hezekiah provide the rationale: the verse comes to establish a second morning for the burning, i.e., the sixteenth of Nisan.

items.text: Abaye and Rava on effectiveness of prohibited actions
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava on effectiveness of prohibited actions
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that any action prohibited by the Torah is effective (מהני), otherwise lashes would be meaningless; Rava counters that it is not effective, and lashes are purely for violating God's command.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asserts that any action prohibited by the Torah is effective (מהני), otherwise lashes would be meaningless.
Rava counters that the action is not effective, and lashes are purely for violating God's command.

items.text: Challenge to Rava from the mishnah of the rapist
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava from the mishnah of the rapist
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: a rapist who divorces his wife, if he is an Israelite, he must remarry her and is not flogged. This challenges Rava, who held that one who violates a negative commandment is flogged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava by citing a baraita: a rapist who divorces his wife, if he is an Israelite, must remarry her and is not flogged, contradicting Rava's principle that one who violates a negative commandment is flogged.

items.text: Rava's answer and Abaye's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's answer and Abaye's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava deflects the challenge by noting the verse 'all his days' teaches that he must always remarry her, so the positive commandment overrides the negative. Abaye explains that without that verse, one might think it is optional, so the verse teaches it is mandatory.

sub.desc_en: Rava deflects the challenge by noting that the verse 'כל ימיו' (all his days) teaches that he must always remarry her, so the positive commandment overrides the negative.
Abaye explains that without the verse 'כל ימיו', one might think the remarriage is optional, so the verse teaches it is mandatory.

items.text: Alternate version: challenge to Abaye
items.text_en: Alternate version: challenge to Abaye
items.desc_en: An alternate version of the baraita states that if the rapist is a priest, he is flogged and does not remarry. This challenges Abaye, who held that one is not flogged for violating a negative commandment attached to a positive one.

sub.desc_en: An alternate version of the baraita is cited, stating that if the rapist is a priest he is flogged and does not remarry, which challenges Abaye's position.

items.text: Abaye's answer and Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's answer and Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye answers that the verse 'all his days' teaches the positive commandment, so the priest is flogged because he cannot remarry. Rava explains that without that verse, one might think he is flogged and then remarries, so the verse makes it a negative commandment attached to a positive one, for which one is not flogged.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the verse 'כל ימיו' (all his days) teaches the positive commandment to stand and remarry, so the priest is flogged because he cannot remarry.

Rava explains that without the verse, one might think he is flogged and then remarries, so the verse makes it a negative commandment attached to a positive one (לאו שניתק לעשה), for which one is not flogged.

items.text: Challenge to Rava from terumah from inferior produce
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava from terumah from inferior produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava from the law of terumah: one may not separate from inferior produce for superior produce, but if he did, it is valid. This shows the action is effective, contradicting Rava's view that violating a negative commandment invalidates the action.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava from the law of terumah: one may not separate from inferior produce for superior produce, as the verse says 'from all its fat' (מִכׇּל חֶלְבּוֹ), implying only from the best, not from inferior.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah: one may not separate from inferior for superior, but if he did, it is valid — showing the action is effective.
The Gemara concludes that this is a refutation of Rava's position, since the action is effective despite violating a negative commandment.

items.text: Rava's answer and Abaye's explanation
items.text_en: Rava's answer and Abaye's explanation
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the case follows Rabbi Ila, who derives from a verse that such terumah is valid. Abaye explains that without that verse, one might think it is merely a mitzvah to choose the best, but not a sin to do otherwise.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the case of terumah from bad to good is different, following Rabbi Ila's derivation from a verse that such terumah is valid.
Abaye explains that without the verse, one might think it is merely a mitzvah to choose the best, but not a sin to do otherwise; the verse teaches that it is indeed a sin.

items.text: Challenge to Abaye from terumah from one species for another
items.text_en: Challenge to Abaye from terumah from one species for another
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye from the law that one may not separate from one species for another, and if he did, it is invalid. This contradicts Abaye's view that violating a negative commandment does not invalidate the action.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye from the law that one may not separate terumah from one species for another, and if he did, it is invalid, contradicting Abaye's view that violating a negative commandment does not invalidate the action.

items.text: Abaye's answer and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's answer and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye answers that the verse 'their first' teaches that each species requires its own first portion. Rava explains that without that verse, one might think that only wine and oil, which share the term 'chelev', cannot be mixed, but other grains could be, so the verse teaches they must be separate.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the case of separating תרומה (priestly portion) from one species for another is different because the verse 'רֵאשִׁיתָם' (their first) teaches that each species requires its own first portion, and Rabbi Ila similarly derives this from 'רֵאשִׁית' (first).

Rava explains that without the verse 'רֵאשִׁית' (first), one might think that only wine and oil, which share the term 'חֵלֶב' (best), cannot be mixed, but other grains could be, so the verse teaches that each species must have its own best portion.

An alternative version states that for wine and grain, where 'חֵלֶב' (best) is written only once, one might have thought it is permitted to separate from one for the other, so the Merciful One writes 'רֵאשִׁית' (first) to prohibit this.

items.text: Challenge to Abaye from devoted property
items.text_en: Challenge to Abaye from devoted property
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye from the law of devoted property (charamim): they cannot be sold or redeemed, but must be given to the priest. This shows the action is ineffective, contradicting Abaye's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to Abaye from the law of devoted property (חרָמִים), which cannot be sold or redeemed, showing the transgression is ineffective.
Abaye answers that the case of devoted property is different because the verse says 'קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים הוּא' (it is most holy), meaning it remains in its original state and cannot be changed.

items.text: Challenge to Rava from temurah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava from temurah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's position by citing temurah: the Torah says 'lo yachalifenu' yet the animal is consecrated and one receives lashes, showing the prohibition does not prevent effectiveness.

items.text: Rava's answer: the verse 'vehaya hu utemurato'
items.text_en: Rava's answer: the verse 'vehaya hu utemurato'
items.desc_en: Rava deflects the challenge by noting that the Torah explicitly says 'vehaya hu utemurato yihyeh kodesh', which teaches that the temurah takes effect despite the prohibition.

items.text: Challenge to Abaye from firstborn
items.text_en: Challenge to Abaye from firstborn
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye: the Torah says 'lo tifdeh' regarding a firstborn, yet the Mishnah teaches that firstborns have redemption and their temurot have redemption, showing the prohibition does not prevent effectiveness.

items.text: Abaye's answer: the word 'hem'
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: the word 'hem'
items.desc_en: Abaye answers that the verse says 'hem' regarding firstborn and tithe, meaning they remain in their original state and cannot be redeemed or exchanged.

items.text: Discussion of the word 'hem' and the source for the law of mixtures
items.text_en: Discussion of the word 'hem' and the source for the law of mixtures
items.desc_en: Rava questions the purpose of 'hem' and derives that it teaches that firstborn and tithe are offered and their temurot are not offered. Abaye derives this from 'im shor im seh laHashem hu'. The Gemara then discusses the source for the rule that offerings do not nullify each other, citing Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan.

items.text: Challenge to Abaye from tithe
items.text_en: Challenge to Abaye from tithe
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye with tithe: the Torah says 'lo yiga'el' yet the Mishnah teaches that tithe has redemption and its temurah has redemption, showing the prohibition does not prevent effectiveness.

items.text: Abaye's answer: gezerah shavah 'avarah' 'avarah' from firstborn
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: gezerah shavah 'avarah' 'avarah' from firstborn
items.desc_en: Abaye answers that tithe is learned via a gezerah shavah of 'avarah' from firstborn, so the same rule applies.

items.text: Challenge to Rava from terumah before bikurim
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava from terumah before bikurim
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava with the case of one who gives terumah before bikurim: the Torah says 'lo te'acher' yet the Mishnah rules that what he did is done. Rava answers with the verse 'mikol ma'asroteichem tarimu terumah'. Abaye questions this with a case of a heap, and the Gemara explains the distinction between a heap and stalks based on the concept of 'digun'.

items.text: Challenge to Rava from a widow marrying a High Priest
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava from a widow marrying a High Priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava with the case of a widow marrying a High Priest: the Torah says 'lo yikach' yet the Mishnah rules that the child follows the defective parent. Rava answers with the verse 'lo yechalel zar'o'. Abaye notes that the verse could have said 'lo yachel' and derives that it applies to both him and her.

items.text: Challenge to Rava from dedicating blemished animals to the altar
items.text_en: Challenge to Rava from dedicating blemished animals to the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava with one who dedicates blemished animals to the altar: the Torah says 'lo takrivu' yet the Mishnah rules that what he did is done. Rava answers with the verse 'ulneder lo yeratzeh', meaning it is not accepted but is consecrated. Abaye explains that without this verse one might think it is valid despite the transgression.

items.text: Beginning of challenge from dedicating unblemished animals to the Temple treasury
items.text_en: Beginning of challenge from dedicating unblemished animals to the Temple treasury
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new challenge to Rava from the case of one who dedicates unblemished animals to the Temple treasury (bedek habayit).

items.text: First challenge to Rava: consecrating unblemished animals for Bedek HaBayit
items.text_en: First challenge to Rava: consecrating unblemished animals for Bedek HaBayit
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse and a Mishnah to challenge Rava: one who consecrates unblemished animals for Temple upkeep violates a negative commandment, yet the act is valid. This is a refutation of Rava's position.

items.text: Rava's answer: blemished animals are permitted for the altar
items.text_en: Rava's answer: blemished animals are permitted for the altar
items.desc_en: Rava responds that the case is different because blemished animals are permitted for the altar, so unblemished animals for Bedek HaBayit are also permitted by analogy.

items.text: Second challenge to Rava: theft
items.text_en: Second challenge to Rava: theft
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava from the law of theft: one who steals and changes the object pays according to the time of theft, despite the negative commandment 'Do not steal.' This is a refutation of Rava.

items.text: Rava's answer and Abaye's objection regarding theft
items.text_en: Rava's answer and Abaye's objection regarding theft
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the verse 'asher gazal' teaches that payment is as at the time of theft. Abaye objects that this verse is needed to teach that one adds a fifth only for one's own theft, not for a father's theft.

items.text: Third challenge to Rava: returning collateral
items.text_en: Third challenge to Rava: returning collateral
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava from the law of collateral: one must return a pillow at night and a plow by day, despite the negative commandment 'Do not enter his house to take his pledge.' This is a refutation of Rava.

items.text: Rava's answer and Abaye's explanation regarding collateral
items.text_en: Rava's answer and Abaye's explanation regarding collateral
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the verse 'hashev tashiv' teaches the obligation to return. Abaye explains that without this verse, one might think the return is optional; the verse teaches it is mandatory.

items.text: Fourth challenge: pe'ah, now a refutation of Abaye
items.text_en: Fourth challenge: pe'ah, now a refutation of Abaye
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye from the law of pe'ah: one who fails to leave pe'ah from standing grain may do so from sheaves or even from the heap, despite the negative commandment. This is a refutation of Abaye.

items.text: Abaye's answer and Rava's alternative explanation regarding pe'ah
items.text_en: Abaye's answer and Rava's alternative explanation regarding pe'ah
items.desc_en: Abaye answers that the verse 'ta'azov' (leave) is extra, teaching that the obligation applies even after harvest. Rava counters that this refers to another case of leaving, like one who abandons his vineyard, as taught in a baraita.

items.text: Conclusion: the dispute is about fixed interest (ribbit ketzutzah)
items.text_en: Conclusion: the dispute is about fixed interest (ribbit ketzutzah)
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi: given all these answers, what is the actual dispute between Abaye and Rava? The Gemara answers that they disagree about fixed interest, as per Rabbi Elazar's statement that fixed interest is collected by judges.

items.text: Dispute over recovering fixed interest through court
items.text_en: Dispute over recovering fixed interest through court
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar regarding whether fixed interest can be recovered through court. Rabbi Yochanan argues it cannot, citing verses that liken interest-takers to murderers, who are not given the opportunity for restitution. Rabbi Elazar holds that it can be recovered, based on the verse 'and your brother shall live with you'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the statement that fixed interest (ריבית קצוצה) cannot be recovered through court, citing Rabbi Yochanan's position.
The Gemara questions whether the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar is based on reasoning or on verses.

Rabbi Yitzchak explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: the verse 'בַּנֶּשֶׁךְ נָתַן... וָחָי לֹא יִחְיֶה' (he gave with interest... he shall not live) indicates that the prohibition is for life, not for restitution.
Rav Acha bar Adda provides an additional verse supporting Rabbi Yochanan: 'וְיָרֵאתָ מֵּאֱלֹהֶיךָ... אֲנִי ה׳' (and you shall fear your God... I am the Lord) — given for awe, not for restitution.
Rava cites a verse comparing interest-takers to murderers, arguing that just as murderers are not given the opportunity for restitution, so too interest-takers cannot recover the interest.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains Rabbi Elazar's reasoning: the verse 'וְחֵי אָחִיךָ עִמָּךְ' (and your brother shall live with you) implies that the interest must be returned so that the borrower can live with you.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's source for recovering interest
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's source for recovering interest
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains Rabbi Elazar's reasoning: the verse 'and your brother shall live with you' implies that one must return the interest so that the borrower can live.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains Rabbi Elazar's source for recovering interest: the verse 'וְחֵי אָחִיךָ עִמָּךְ' (and your brother shall live with you) implies that the lender must return the interest so the borrower can live.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's dispute over shinui koneh
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's dispute over shinui koneh
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding interest is actually about the principle of shinui koneh (change of ownership). Abaye holds that if the borrower buys an item from the lender with the interest money, the interest is not returned, while Rava argues it must be returned. A case is brought where a borrower gave a cloak worth five zuz for four zuz of debt, and Abaye says only four zuz are recovered, while Rava says all five.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the dispute about interest is not about the effectiveness of transgression, then about what do Abaye and Rava disagree? It answers: They disagree about the principle of שינוי קונה (change of ownership).
An alternative version states: In the case of fixed interest, according to Abaye the interest is not returned, while according to Rava it is returned.

The Gemara objects: But Abaye also holds that fixed interest is repossessed by the court, as shown by his ruling that when a borrower gave a cloak worth five zuz for four zuz of interest, only four zuz are recovered, while Rava says all five are recovered because it all came as interest.
The Gemara resolves: Rather, when Abaye and Rava disagree, it is specifically about the principle of שינוי קונה (change of ownership).

items.text: Prohibition of consecrating blemished animals
items.text_en: Prohibition of consecrating blemished animals
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who consecrates blemished animals for the altar violates five prohibitions: not to offer, not to consecrate, not to slaughter, not to sprinkle the blood, and not to burn the fat. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds the prohibition of receiving the blood.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by questioning the verse 'כל אשר בו מום לא תקריבו' (whatever has a blemish, you shall not offer) and explains that it teaches the prohibition of consecrating blemished animals, not just slaughtering.
The baraita lists the five prohibitions violated by consecrating blemished animals, and adds that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda includes the prohibition of receiving the blood.

items.text: Derivation of prohibitions from verses
items.text_en: Derivation of prohibitions from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the derivation of each prohibition from the verses. The verse 'bal takrivu' teaches not to slaughter, and 'isheh lo titnu' includes even partial burning. The sprinkling of blood is derived from 'al hamizbe'ach' and 'laHashem' includes the scapegoat.

sub.desc_en: Mar cites the baraita that derives the prohibition of slaughtering a blemished animal from the verse 'בל תקריבו' (do not offer), since the prohibition of consecration is already stated above.
The baraita derives that the prohibition 'אשה לא תתנו מהם' (you shall not give a fire-offering from them) includes even partial burning, using the word 'מהם' (from them).

sub.text: Baraita on blood sprinkling and scapegoat
sub.text_en: Baraita on blood sprinkling and scapegoat
sub.desc_en: The baraita derives the prohibition of sprinkling blood from 'על המזבח' (on the altar) and includes the scapegoat from 'לה׳' (to the Lord).

items.text: Exclusion of scapegoat from outer slaughter prohibition
items.text_en: Exclusion of scapegoat from outer slaughter prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'laHashem' includes the scapegoat, and resolves that the verse 'el petach ohel mo'ed' limits the prohibition to animals fit for the Tent of Meeting. The scapegoat is excluded because it is not designated for God.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'לַה׳' (to God) includes the scapegoat, citing a baraita that 'קרבן' (offering) might include Temple property.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וְאֶל פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' (to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting) limits the prohibition to animals fit for the Tent of Meeting, excluding the scapegoat.
The Gemara resolves that the scapegoat is excluded because it is not designated for God, as the phrase 'לַה׳' (to God) limits the prohibition to animals uniquely dedicated to God.

items.text: Rava's distinction and the scapegoat's blemish status
items.text_en: Rava's distinction and the scapegoat's blemish status
items.desc_en: Rava explains the difference in interpretation: in the context of outer slaughter, 'el petach' includes and 'laHashem' excludes, while here 'isheh' excludes and 'laHashem' includes. The Gemara then questions whether the scapegoat is considered blemished, and concludes that the lot determines it only for a fit animal.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains the exegetical difference: in the outer slaughter context, 'אל פתח' (to the entrance) includes and 'לה׳' (to the Lord) excludes, while here 'אשה' (fire-offering) excludes and 'לה׳' includes.
The Gemara infers that without the verse 'לה׳', one would have thought the scapegoat is considered blemished and thus excluded.
The Gemara resolves that the lot determines the scapegoat only for a fit animal, so a blemished animal is not subject to the lot.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who holds the scapegoat is fit
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who holds the scapegoat is fit
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests the ruling follows Chanan HaMitzri, who holds that even blood in a cup can be paired, but is rejected because Chanan might still require a lottery. Rav Yosef then suggests it follows Rabbi Shimon, who allows bringing a partner without a lottery if one dies. Rava offers an alternative: the case is where the scapegoat became blemished on the same day and was redeemed onto another.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests that the anonymous ruling follows Chanan HaMitzri, who holds that even blood in a cup can be paired with a partner.
The Gemara objects that even if Chanan HaMitzri does not require disqualification, he might still require a lottery, which is absent in the case.
Rav Yosef alternatively suggests the ruling follows Rabbi Shimon, who allows bringing a partner without a lottery if one of the pair dies.
Rava resolves the case by explaining it involves a scapegoat that became blemished on the same day and was redeemed onto another, avoiding the need for a lottery.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's intent
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement that one is liable for offering a blemished animal even if it became blemished after designation is to counter a possible assumption that once the animal's status as a sacrifice is forgotten, there would be no liability.

items.text: Dispute over the source for receiving the blood
items.text_en: Dispute over the source for receiving the blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that the prohibition 'lo takrivu' includes receiving the blood, and the Tanna Kamma's alternative derivation for the same verse. It also addresses the Tanna Kamma's use of the verse for a different halakha regarding Noahides.

items.text: Alternative version of the dispute
items.text_en: Alternative version of the dispute
items.desc_en: A second version of the debate is presented, where Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda derives receiving the blood from 'lo takrivu' and sprinkling from 'al hamizbe'ach', while the Rabbis use the verse for a private altar (bamat yachid). The Gemara explains the Rabbis' additional need for the verse to exclude accepting offerings from Noahides.

items.text: Reish Lakish's challenge
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's challenge
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges the Mishnah's ruling, suggesting that it only applies to a previously unblemished animal that became blemished, not to one blemished from the start, which he compares to a mere palm tree.

items.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef objects by citing the verse 'sarua vekalut' which are inherently blemished, implying that the Mishnah does include animals blemished from the start.

items.text: Reish Lakish's second suggestion
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's second suggestion
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish suggests that the Mishnah might only apply to temurah, where sanctity can take effect on a permanently blemished animal.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution and debate
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution and debate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Yannai's ruling that one who consecrates a blemished animal is liable for five prohibitions, and if it were only temurah, there would be six. He concludes that the Mishnah must refer to an animal blemished from the start, and the reason for liability is the disgrace of choosing a blemished animal over unblemished ones.

items.text: Rava's extension and supporting baraitha
items.text_en: Rava's extension and supporting baraitha
items.desc_en: Rava extends the principle: since the reason for liability is the disgrace, one is even liable for consecrating a blemished animal for the value of libations. A baraitha supports Rava's view.

items.text: Opening Tannaitic exposition on "nedavah" and "neder"
items.text_en: Opening Tannaitic exposition on "nedavah" and "neder"
items.desc_en: The Tanna derives from the verse that "nedavah" refers to Temple upkeep and "neder" to altar sacrifices, with Rabbi adding that "lo yeratzeh" speaks of the animal's own acceptance.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma derives from the verse that 'נְדָבָה' (freewill offering) refers to Temple upkeep and 'נֶדֶר' (vow) to altar sacrifices.
Rabbi adds that the phrase 'לֹא יֵרָצֶה' (it shall not be accepted) speaks of the animal's own acceptance, not its value.

items.text: Gemara's question on the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the difference is between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi, concluding that they argue about whether one is liable for consecrating the value of libations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi differ, since their positions appear identical.
The Gemara resolves that they argue about liability for consecrating the value of libations: the Tanna Kamma holds one is liable, while Rabbi holds one is not.

items.text: Derivation regarding unblemished animals for Temple upkeep
items.text_en: Derivation regarding unblemished animals for Temple upkeep
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the word "oto" teaches that one may not dedicate unblemished animals for Temple upkeep, and Rabbi Yehuda adds a negative commandment from the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'אותו' (him) in the verse teaches, since it was already used for another derivation.
A baraita is cited: the word 'אותו' teaches that one may not dedicate unblemished animals for Temple upkeep (בדק הבית), and doing so violates a positive commandment.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that a negative commandment is also violated, derived from the word 'לֵאמֹר' (saying) in the verse.

items.text: Derivation of the negative commandment
items.text_en: Derivation of the negative commandment
items.desc_en: Rabbi asks Bar Kappara the source, who explains from "leimor" that it is a negative commandment, and the school of Rabbi says "lo emor".

sub.desc_en: Rabbi asks Bar Kappara for the source of the negative commandment.
Bar Kappara explains that the word 'לֵאמֹר' (to say) implies 'לֹא' (no) was said in the matter, deriving a negative commandment.
The school of Rabbi derives the negative commandment from 'לֹא אֱמוֹר' (do not say), a play on 'לֵאמֹר'.

items.text: Dispute about offering blemished animals
items.text_en: Dispute about offering blemished animals
items.desc_en: Rava says one who offers limbs of blemished animals violates two prohibitions, Abaye counters that there is no lashes for a general prohibition, and a baraita refutes Abaye.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports a dispute: Rava says one who offers limbs of blemished animals violates two prohibitions — 'בל תקטירו כולו' (do not offer the whole) and 'בל תקטירו מקצתו' (do not offer part of it).
Abaye objects that one is not flogged for a general prohibition (לאו שבכללות) that encompasses multiple distinct acts.
A baraita is cited: one who consecrates blemished animals for the altar violates five prohibitions, which refutes Abaye's position.
Abaye tries to reject the refutation by claiming the baraita refers to multiple people (גברי), but the gemara notes the singular verb 'עובר' disproves this, confirming the refutation.

items.text: Abaye's alternative resolution and final refutation
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative resolution and final refutation
items.desc_en: Abaye attempts to replace one prohibition with another, but the Gemara shows inconsistency with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, and a second version confirms the refutation.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes replacing the prohibition of 'הקטרת מקצתו' (offering part of a blemished animal) with 'קבלת הדם' (receiving the blood) to salvage his position.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda holds the prohibition of 'קבלת הדם' (receiving the blood), but the first Tanna does not, making Abaye's substitution inconsistent.
An alternative version states that the latter clause of the baraita is Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, while the beginning is the Rabbis, confirming the inconsistency.
The Gemara concludes that Abaye's position is definitively refuted (תיוּבְתָּא).

items.text: Mishnah: Priests and Israelites effect temurah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Priests and Israelites effect temurah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that priests and Israelites can effect temurah with their own animals, but priests cannot with chatat, asham, or bekhor, and Rabbi Akiva argues that bekhor is like chatat and asham.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that priests and Israelites may effect temurah with their own animals, but priests may not do so with a chatat, asham, or bekhor.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri asks why priests do not effect temurah with a bekhor.
Rabbi Akiva answers that just as a chatat and asham, which are gifts to the priest, cannot be used for temurah, so too a bekhor, also a gift to the priest, cannot be used for temurah.

items.text: Gemara: Selling a firstborn animal
items.text_en: Gemara: Selling a firstborn animal
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman limits the Mishnah's ruling about selling a firstborn to the present time, but Rava objects with a baraita, and Rav Nachman defends his position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah from Bekhorot that a firstborn animal may be sold alive when unblemished, and when blemished either alive or slaughtered, and may be used to betroth a woman.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabba bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuha limits the Mishnah's leniency to the present time when the priest has a share in the animal, but when the Temple stands, an unblemished firstborn designated for sacrifice may not be sold alive.
Rava objects by citing the Mishnah's phrase 'alive' but not 'slaughtered' for an unblemished firstborn, arguing this implies the Temple era, proving the priest has a share even then.
Rav Nachman defends his position by reinterpreting the Mishnah as referring entirely to the present time, teaching that even in this era an unblemished firstborn may be sold alive.

items.text: First challenge from a baraita about selling a firstborn
items.text_en: First challenge from a baraita about selling a firstborn
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that states a firstborn may be sold, despite the verse 'you shall not redeem it'. It clarifies that this refers to the time of the Temple, and if the animal is unblemished, implying the priest has a share in it.

items.text: Rejection: the baraita refers to a blemished firstborn
items.text_en: Rejection: the baraita refers to a blemished firstborn
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the baraita's first clause deals with a blemished animal (which may be sold), while the latter clause deals with an unblemished one (whose blood is sprinkled).

items.text: Second challenge from a mishna about a priestess and her slave
items.text_en: Second challenge from a mishna about a priestess and her slave
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya cites a case where a priestess's child and her slave's child are mixed up. The mishna states their firstborns must graze until blemished. The Gemara argues that if the priest has no share in an unblemished firstborn, the treasurer could simply take it, but the mishna implies the priest does have a share.

items.text: First answer: the mishna refers to the present time
items.text_en: First answer: the mishna refers to the present time
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishna deals with the present time (when there is no Temple). The difference between the priestess's child and the slave's child is that the latter, having some priestly status, can remove the firstborn from the priests entirely.

items.text: Alternative formulation of the challenge
items.text_en: Alternative formulation of the challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents another version of the challenge: if the mishna is about the present time, why mention firstborns specifically? Even our own firstborns would graze. So it must be about the Temple period, and if the animal is blemished, why say 'until they become blemished'? So it must be about unblemished animals, and the mishna implies that definite firstborns are not sold.

items.text: Second answer: the mishna refers to the present time, with a different explanation
items.text_en: Second answer: the mishna refers to the present time, with a different explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the mishna indeed deals with the present time. The reason definite firstborns are not sold is that we cannot push them to a priest, as there is no doubt about priesthood. But these doubtful firstborns can be pushed to a priest, as each claims to be a priest.

items.text: Third challenge from Rabbi Shimon's statement about an idolatrous city
items.text_en: Third challenge from Rabbi Shimon's statement about an idolatrous city
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Shimon's statement that 'her animal' excludes a firstborn and tithe animal, and 'her spoil' excludes second tithe money. The Gemara argues that if the priest has no share in an unblemished firstborn, why exclude it from 'her animal'? It could be excluded from 'her spoil' as 'spoil of Heaven'. This implies the priest does have a share.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Shimon refers to a blemished firstborn
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Shimon refers to a blemished firstborn
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon's statement deals with a blemished firstborn. The exclusion 'her animal' means an animal that is eaten in the manner of 'her animal' (i.e., sold in the market), which excludes firstborn and tithe animals that are not eaten in that manner, as per the mishna that they are not sold in the market.

items.text: Fourth challenge from the verse about me'ilah
items.text_en: Fourth challenge from the verse about me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute about the verse 'and commits a trespass against the Lord', which includes light sacrifices. Ben Azzai says it includes peace-offerings, and Abba Yosei ben Dosai says he only meant a firstborn. The Gemara argues that if the priest has no share in an unblemished firstborn, why include it? It must be that the priest does have a share.

items.text: Abaye's initial statement
items.text_en: Abaye's initial statement
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that the case of a firstborn animal in the Diaspora is treated as a temim (unblemished) animal, and follows Rabbi Shimon's view that if unblemished animals come, they may be offered.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the case involves a תם (unblemished) firstborn outside the land, following Rabbi Shimon's view that if brought unblemished they may be sacrificed.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: An objection is raised based on a statement by Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri, who argues that a firstborn animal is different from a sin-offering or guilt-offering because one can benefit from it while alive. The Gemara clarifies that this refers to a blemished animal, not a temim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri argues that a firstborn is comparable to a sin-offering or guilt-offering because one acquires rights in it during its lifetime, implying it must be unblemished.

items.text: Ravina's resolution
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution
items.desc_en: Ravina resolves the objection by stating that the case is indeed a firstborn in the Diaspora, following Rabbi Shimon's view that if unblemished animals come, they may be offered.

sub.desc_en: Ravina answers that the baraita also refers to a firstborn outside the land, following Rabbi Shimon's view.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about temurah for a firstborn
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about temurah for a firstborn
items.desc_en: A dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is presented: the Tanna Kamma says that a firstborn in the kohen's house can be exchanged, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says that once it comes into the kohen's possession, it cannot be exchanged. The Gemara questions whether this implies the kohen has a right to the animal.

items.text: Resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by attributing the two views to Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva, respectively.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by attributing the two positions to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva respectively.

items.text: Rav Hisda's ruling on kohen to Israelite
items.text_en: Rav Hisda's ruling on kohen to Israelite
items.desc_en: Rav Hisda rules that a kohen may give a firstborn to another kohen, but not to an Israelite, because the Israelite might cause a blemish and then claim it was given by a kohen.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that the allowance to sell a firstborn applies only from priest to priest, but from priest to Israelite it is forbidden, lest the Israelite blemish it and bring it to a sage claiming the priest gave it to him already blemished.

items.text: Objection from Rav's statement
items.text_en: Objection from Rav's statement
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: if a kohen gives a firstborn to an Israelite, would a sage permit it? Rav said that a firstborn is only inspected for an Israelite if a kohen is present.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: would a sage permit such a thing? Rav said that a firstborn is not examined for an Israelite unless a priest is present.

items.text: Rav Huna's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Huna's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that the reason an Israelite is prohibited is because it appears as if the kohen is assisting in the granary.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that the reason an Israelite is forbidden is because it appears like a priest assisting at the threshing floor.

items.text: Story of Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Story of Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra visits Rav Ashi's house and is offered meat from a firstborn. He questions the source, and the hosts explain they bought it from a kohen. Mar Zutra then cites Rav Huna's ruling, but the hosts argue that since they bought it, it is different. The Gemara then presents two alternative explanations for the distinction.

items.text: Opening aphorism
items.text_en: Opening aphorism
items.desc_en: A brief saying: 'A lamp is better than a reading' (Butzina tav mikara), likely a scribal or introductory note.

items.text: Mishnah: Permitted temurah exchanges
items.text_en: Mishnah: Permitted temurah exchanges
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists that one may exchange from flock to cattle, cattle to flock, rams to goats, goats to rams, males to females, females to males, unblemished for blemished, and blemished for unblemished, citing the verse 'lo yachalifenu velo yamir oto tov bera o ra betov' and explaining that 'tov bera' refers to blemished animals whose consecration preceded their blemish.

items.text: Gemara: Source for the Mishnah's list
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the Mishnah's list
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of these rules. A baraita derives from 'behemah bivhemah' that all these exchanges are valid, and then limits the verse 'tov bera' to cases where consecration preceded the blemish, excluding animals blemished before consecration.

items.text: Abaye and Rava: Derivation of the rule from the verse
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava: Derivation of the rule from the verse
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the extra 'betov' in the verse teaches that only an animal that was originally unblemished (tov me'ikaro) can effect temurah, not one blemished from the start. Rava argues that both instances of 'tov' are superfluous: one teaches that even exchanging for a good animal is punishable, and the other that only originally good animals effect temurah. Abaye counters with a kal vahomer: if exchanging good for bad is punishable, exchanging good for good certainly is. Rava responds that we do not punish based on logical inference, and Abaye retorts that this is not a mere inference, as good is no less than bad.

items.text: Derivation: Exchanging another's animal
items.text_en: Derivation: Exchanging another's animal
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'lo yachalifenu' refers to exchanging with another's animal, while 'lo yamir oto' refers to one's own. The Gemara questions why both are needed, and explains that without 'lo yamir oto' one might think only a swap (this goes out, that comes in) is punishable, but consecrating both simultaneously is not. The Gemara then clarifies the case of another's animal: it must be where the owner of the consecrated animal said 'whoever wishes to exchange may come and exchange'.

items.text: Mishnah: One for two, two for one
items.text_en: Mishnah: One for two, two for one
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may exchange one animal for two, two for one, one for a hundred, or a hundred for one. Rabbi Shimon disagrees, saying only one for one, based on the verse 'vehayah hu utemurato yihyeh kodesh' — just as 'hu' is singular, so the temurah must be singular.

items.text: Gemara: Source and debate on one-for-two
items.text_en: Gemara: Source and debate on one-for-two
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where the Sages derive from 'behemah bivhemah' that one may exchange one for two, etc., while Rabbi Shimon argues that 'behemah bivhemah' implies one animal for one animal, not one for many or many for one. The Sages counter that 'behemah rabbah' shows 'behemah' can refer to many. Rabbi Shimon responds that 'behemah rabbah' is a special case, not 'behemah' alone. The Gemara then notes that Rabbi Shimon's original reason was from 'hu', but when he saw the Sages deriving from 'behemah bivhemah', he offered that as an additional support.

items.text: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan: Sequential temurot
items.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan: Sequential temurot
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says Rabbi Shimon agrees that one may exchange and then exchange again, because the first sanctity remains. Rabbi Yochanan says just as one cannot exchange two for one, so one cannot exchange sequentially. Two baraisot support each opinion: one supports Rabbi Yochanan, the other supports Reish Lakish, deriving from 'vehayah hu utemurato' that even a hundred exchanges are valid.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's query: Asham and temurah
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's query: Asham and temurah
