items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that regarding the offspring of an Asham, where there is no name of Olah on the mother, Rabbi Elazar agrees that only its monetary value is brought for an Olah, but the animal itself is not sacrificed.

items.text: Abaye's objection and Rava's answer from the Pesach case
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Rava's answer from the Pesach case
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbi Elazar's requirement for a name of Olah on the mother, citing a baraita where a female designated for Pesach gives birth, and Rabbi Elazar says the offspring itself is brought as Shelamim after Pesach, even though the mother had no name of Shelamim. Rava responds that after Pesach is different because the surplus of Pesach itself is brought as Shelamim.

items.text: Question and answer on whether Rabbi Elazar disputes the first clause
items.text_en: Question and answer on whether Rabbi Elazar disputes the first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if Rabbi Elazar should also dispute the first clause of the baraita (before Pesach). Rava responds that indeed he does dispute it.

items.text: Abaye's alternative explanation: the offspring follows the surplus
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative explanation: the offspring follows the surplus
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that Rabbi Elazar does not dispute the first clause; rather, there is a principle that the offspring goes where the surplus goes. After Pesach, the surplus is brought as Shelamim, so the offspring is also brought as Shelamim. Before Pesach, the mother was designated for the value of Pesach, so the offspring also goes for the value of Pesach.

items.text: Rav Ukva bar Chama's objection from another baraita
items.text_en: Rav Ukva bar Chama's objection from another baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Ukva bar Chama objects to Abaye's reasoning, citing a baraita where a female designated for Pesach and her offspring are sold and the proceeds used for Pesach, but Rabbi Elazar says the offspring itself is brought as Pesach. This shows that even when the mother is for value, Rabbi Elazar does not place the offspring in the mother's status.

items.text: Ravina's resolution: the case involves a pregnant animal
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution: the case involves a pregnant animal
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the baraita deals with a pregnant animal. Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Yochanan's view that a fetus is not considered a limb of its mother, so the mother is not sanctified with bodily sanctity, but the offspring is. Mar Zutra bar Rav Mari supports this from the language 'she and her offspring'.

items.text: Gemara's discussion of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement about Rabbi Elazar's view
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement about Rabbi Elazar's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina states that Rabbi Elazar agrees that if one consecrates a female for an asham, her offspring cannot be offered as an asham. The Gemara questions why this is not obvious, and explains that without this statement one might have thought Rabbi Elazar's reasoning is based on the offspring's fitness for sacrifice, not on the mother's sanctity. The Gemara then clarifies why the case of asham needed to be stated separately from the case of olah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina states that Rabbi Elazar concedes that the offspring of a female consecrated for an asham cannot be offered as an asham.
The Gemara explains that without this statement, one might have thought Rabbi Elazar's reasoning is based on the offspring's fitness for sacrifice, so the statement teaches otherwise.
The Gemara objects that the teaching should have been about the offspring not being offered as an olah, which would imply the same for asham.
The Gemara resolves that teaching about olah alone might have led to a mistaken inference about asham, so the separate statement is necessary.

items.text: Mishnah: The law of one who consecrates a female for an asham
items.text_en: Mishnah: The law of one who consecrates a female for an asham
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one consecrates a female for an asham, it must graze until it becomes blemished, then be sold, and with its proceeds an asham is brought. If his asham was already offered, the proceeds go to the Temple treasury. Rabbi Shimon says it may be sold without a blemish.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of one who consecrates a female for an asham: it grazes until blemished, is sold, and an asham is brought with its proceeds; if the asham was already offered, the proceeds go to the Temple treasury.
Rabbi Shimon says the female may be sold without a blemish.

items.text: Gemara: Why require a blemish? The principle of consecration for value vs. body
items.text_en: Gemara: Why require a blemish? The principle of consecration for value vs. body
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah requires the animal to become blemished before sale, since it is already unfit for sacrifice. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that when one consecrates a female for an asham, the sanctity of value descends upon it, and consequently sanctity of the body also descends. Rava deduces from this that if one consecrates a male for its value, it becomes consecrated with sanctity of the body. An amoraic dispute between Rav Kahana and Rava is recorded, and Rava retracts in favor of Rav Kahana based on Rav's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah requires the animal to become blemished before sale, since it is already unfit for sacrifice.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that when one consecrates a female for an asham, the sanctity of value descends upon it, and consequently sanctity of the body also descends.
Rava deduces from Rav's statement that if one consecrates a male for its value, it becomes consecrated with sanctity of the body.
An amoraic dispute is recorded: Rav Kahana says it becomes consecrated with sanctity of the body, while Rava says it does not.
The Gemara reports that Rava retracted in favor of Rav Kahana, based on Rav's statement.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's view and the principle of 'not fit for its body'
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's view and the principle of 'not fit for its body'
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin asks Rabbi Yochanan why Rabbi Shimon says the animal can be sold without a blemish, given the principle of sanctity descending. Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Shimon holds that anything not fit for sacrifice itself does not receive sanctity of the body. This is supported by a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says that an asham brought at the wrong age is not consecrated at all. The Gemara distinguishes this from a case of a time-deficient animal, which Rabbi Shimon does consider consecrated, learning from the firstborn.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Avin's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin asks Rabbi Yochanan why Rabbi Shimon permits selling the animal without a blemish, given the principle that sanctity of the body should descend along with sanctity of the money.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Shimon follows his own principle: anything not fit for sacrifice itself does not receive sanctity of the body.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon rules that an asham brought at the wrong age is not consecrated at all, supporting the principle that unfit animals do not receive sanctity of the body.
The Gemara objects that a time-deficient animal (מחוסר זמן) is also not fit now, yet Rabbi Shimon considers it consecrated; the Gemara answers that a time-deficient animal will be fit tomorrow.

The Gemara objects that an asham brought at the wrong age will also be fit next year, yet Rabbi Shimon says it is not consecrated; the Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon's ruling on time-deficient animals is derived from the firstborn (בכור).

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda reports in the name of Rabbi Shimon that a time-deficient animal enters the pen for tithing and is like a firstborn, which is consecrated before its time and offered after its time.

items.text: Beginning of a baraita: One who consecrates a female for an olah
items.text_en: Beginning of a baraita: One who consecrates a female for an olah
items.desc_en: The baraita begins to discuss the case of one who consecrates a female for an olah, which will be elaborated in the following segments.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the case of one who consecrates a female animal for his olah offering.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon's ruling on temurah for Passover and guilt offerings
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon's ruling on temurah for Passover and guilt offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for a Passover or guilt offering, one can effect temurah. Rabbi Shimon disagrees, arguing that only an animal that can graze until blemished (i.e., not designated for a specific time-bound offering) can effect temurah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that for a Passover or guilt offering, one can effect temurah (exchange).
Rabbi Shimon disagrees, ruling that only for a burnt offering can one effect temurah, but not for a Passover or guilt offering.
Rabbi Shimon explains his principle: only an animal that can graze until blemished (i.e., not designated for a time-bound offering) can effect temurah.

items.text: Rabbi's critique: Passover's leftover becomes a peace offering
items.text_en: Rabbi's critique: Passover's leftover becomes a peace offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi argues that Rabbi Shimon's view is not applicable to the Passover offering because its leftover (if not needed) is offered as a peace offering, which can effect temurah. The Gemara questions why Rabbi does not similarly reject Rabbi Shimon's view for the guilt offering, and explains that Rabbi holds like the Rabbis that leftover funds go to communal offerings, which cannot effect temurah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi states that he does not accept Rabbi Shimon's view regarding the Passover offering, because its leftover is offered as a peace offering.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi does not also reject Rabbi Shimon's view for the guilt offering, whose leftover is offered as a burnt offering.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi holds like the Rabbis, that leftover funds go to communal offerings, which cannot effect temurah.

items.text: Initial assumption: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning for a female animal designated as a burnt offering
items.text_en: Initial assumption: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning for a female animal designated as a burnt offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that Rabbi Shimon's reasoning for allowing temurah when one designates a female animal for a burnt offering is because the name 'burnt offering' applies to it in the context of bird offerings (where females are valid).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that Rabbi Shimon's reasoning for allowing temurah when one designates a female animal for a burnt offering is because the name 'burnt offering' applies to it in the context of bird offerings (where females are valid).

items.text: Refutation: Comparison to other cases where the name applies but temurah is not effective
items.text_en: Refutation: Comparison to other cases where the name applies but temurah is not effective
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the initial assumption by comparing to a High Priest who designates a cow for his bullock (which is a male) – the cow should be consecrated because there is a cow for a sin offering? But that is Temple funds, which do not effect temurah. Similarly, an individual who designates a female goat for his sin offering (which is a male) or a prince who designates a female goat for his sin offering – these are different bodies (the person and the offering type are distinct).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the mere existence of a name (e.g., 'cow for a sin offering') sufficed, then a High Priest who designates a cow for his bullock should effect temurah, but this is rejected because it is Temple funds (קדשי בדק הבית), which do not effect temurah.

The Gemara objects further: an individual who designates a male goat for his female goat offering, or a prince who designates a female goat for his male goat offering, should also effect temurah, but these are different bodies (the person and the offering type are distinct).
The Gemara resolves: these are two distinct bodies (the person and the offering type), so the comparison fails.

items.text: Further challenge: If they sinned before appointment, the name applies
items.text_en: Further challenge: If they sinned before appointment, the name applies
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If they sinned before being appointed, then designating a goat for a sin offering would be valid because if they sinned now they would bring a goat. But the Gemara responds: If they did not sin, they are not obligated to bring a goat. Similarly, here (with the female burnt offering), if one does not bring a bird offering, the name does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: If they sinned before being appointed, then designating a goat for a sin offering would be valid because if they sinned now they would bring a goat.
The Gemara responds: If they did not sin, they are not obligated to bring a goat; similarly, here (with the female burnt offering), if one does not bring a bird offering, the name does not apply.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah: bird offerings are valid for a burnt offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah: bird offerings are valid for a burnt offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon holds like Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, who rules that if one vows a burnt offering, he may bring a bird (turtledove or pigeon), so the name 'burnt offering' applies to females as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon holds like Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, who rules that one who vows a burnt offering may bring a bird (turtledove or pigeon), so the name 'burnt offering' applies to females as well.

items.text: Digression: Rabbi Yehoshua's view on consecrated animals and Rabbi Shimon's principle
items.text_en: Digression: Rabbi Yehoshua's view on consecrated animals and Rabbi Shimon's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about one who consecrates his property, including animals fit for the altar. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute how to handle males and females. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba asks Rabbi Yochanan about Rabbi Yehoshua's view: how can females be sold for peace offerings if they were consecrated with bodily sanctity? Rabbi Yochanan answers that Rabbi Yehoshua holds like Rabbi Shimon, who says that anything not fit for its specific purpose does not receive bodily sanctity, citing the case of a female designated for a guilt offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about one who consecrates property containing animals fit for the altar: Rabbi Eliezer says males are sold for burnt offerings and females for peace offerings, while Rabbi Yehoshua says males themselves are offered as burnt offerings and females are sold for peace offerings, with proceeds used for burnt offerings.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba asks Rabbi Yochanan: according to Rabbi Yehoshua, if males themselves are offered as burnt offerings, implying bodily sanctity, then why are females sold for peace offerings rather than requiring pasture until they develop a blemish?

Rabbi Yochanan answers that Rabbi Yehoshua holds like Rabbi Shimon, who rules that anything not fit for its specific purpose does not receive bodily sanctity, citing the case of a female designated for a guilt offering.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of Rabbi Shimon's view on temurah of a female for a burnt-offering
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of Rabbi Shimon's view on temurah of a female for a burnt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that Rabbi Shimon would agree that a female designated for a burnt-offering cannot be made temurah because the name 'burnt-offering' applies to its mother. Rabbi Yehoshua suggests that Rabbi Shimon holds like another Tanna who says he does not make temurah even for his burnt-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that Rabbi Shimon would agree regarding a female for a burnt-offering because the name 'burnt-offering' applies to its mother.
The Gemara objects that we have heard Rabbi Shimon explicitly say that one does make temurah for his burnt-offering.
Rabbi Yehoshua resolves that Rabbi Shimon holds like another Tanna (Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda) who says that even for his burnt-offering he does not make temurah.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute over the fate of temurah of an asham and its offspring
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute over the fate of temurah of an asham and its offspring
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the temurah of an asham, its offspring, and subsequent generations must graze until blemished, then be sold with proceeds for nedavah. Rabbi Eliezer says they die, and Rabbi Elazar says he brings a burnt-offering with their value. The Mishnah then discusses the difference between Rabbi Elazar's view and the Sages regarding the status of the animal as a burnt-offering versus nedavah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that the temurah of an asham, its offspring, and subsequent generations graze until blemished and are sold with proceeds for nedavah, then presents the dissenting views of Rabbi Eliezer (they die) and Rabbi Elazar (he brings a burnt-offering with their value).
The Mishnah adds a parallel case: an asham whose owners died or who have been atoned for also graze until blemished, with the same dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Elazar.
The Mishnah asks: since nedavah is also a burnt-offering, what is the difference between Rabbi Elazar's view and the Sages?

The Mishnah answers: when it comes as a burnt-offering (Rabbi Elazar's view), the owner may perform semikhah, bring his own libations, and if a priest, keeps the service and hide; when it is nedavah (Sages' view), he does not perform semikhah, libations come from the community, and the service and hide belong to the mishmar.

items.text: Gemara: Need for both cases in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Need for both cases in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both cases (asham whose owners died and temurah of asham) are necessary: to show that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling of 'they die' applies only after atonement, and that the Rabbis might agree with him in the case of asham itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that both cases in the Mishnah are necessary.

The Gemara explains that if only the case of asham (whose owners died) were taught, one might think Rabbi Eliezer's ruling of 'they die' applies only there because he decrees after atonement due to before atonement.
The Gemara explains that the case of temurat asham (substitute of an asham) is taught to show that Rabbi Eliezer might agree with the Rabbis there.
The Gemara concludes that both cases are necessary: the Rabbis might agree with Rabbi Eliezer in the case of asham itself, so both are taught.

items.text: Rav Nachman's first version: Dispute after atonement
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's first version: Dispute after atonement
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Rabbah bar Avuh that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis is only after atonement, but before atonement all agree the animal itself is offered as an asham.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports Rabbah bar Avuh's statement that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis applies only after atonement (לאחר כפרה), but before atonement all agree the animal itself is offered as an asham.

items.text: Rava's objection and correction of Rav Nachman's statement
items.text_en: Rava's objection and correction of Rav Nachman's statement
items.desc_en: Rava objects with two points: no atonement comes from something acquired through transgression, and a baraita supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that only the first offspring is offered. The Gemara then corrects Rav Nachman's statement: the dispute is before atonement, and after atonement the animal itself is offered as a burnt-offering. The baraita remains a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman's statement with two points: no atonement comes from something acquired through transgression, and a baraita supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that only the first offspring is offered.
The Gemara corrects Rav Nachman's statement: the dispute is before atonement, and after atonement the animal itself is offered as a burnt-offering.
The Gemara notes that the baraita cited by Rav Chananya remains a difficulty against the corrected version.

items.text: Inquiry about a female designated for asham and its offspring
items.text_en: Inquiry about a female designated for asham and its offspring
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Chiya asks Rabbi Avin bar Kahana whether the offspring of a female designated for an asham may be brought as a burnt-offering. The discussion considers Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's view that Rabbi Elazar would agree, but concludes that Rabbi Elazar's reasoning is not because the name 'burnt-offering' is on the mother, but because the animal is fit for offering. The Gemara cites a baraita that only the value of offspring is used for a burnt-offering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Chiya asks Rabbi Avin bar Kahana whether the offspring of a female designated for an asham may be brought as a burnt-offering.
The Gemara notes that one could resolve the question from Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's statement that Rabbi Elazar would agree, but Rabbi Avin bar Chiya had not heard that teaching.

Rabbi Avin bar Kahana answers that the offspring may be brought as a burnt-offering, but the Gemara questions this, noting that Rabbi Elazar's reasoning applies only when the mother was designated for a burnt-offering, not for an asham.

Rabbi Avin bar Kahana rejects the objection, explaining that Rabbi Elazar's reasoning is not because the name 'burnt-offering' is on the mother, but because the animal is fit for offering, and this offspring is also fit for offering.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states only the value of offspring is used for a burnt-offering, implying the offspring itself is not brought.

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes a previous discussion about a case where an animal gives birth only to females, and a forced resolution is offered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the previous difficulty by positing a forced scenario where the animal gave birth only to females forever.

items.text: Mishnah: Status of substitutes for firstborn and tithe
items.text_en: Mishnah: Status of substitutes for firstborn and tithe
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the substitute of a firstborn or tithe animal, and their offspring, are treated like the original and may be eaten by the owners if blemished. It lists differences between these and other sacrifices: they cannot be sold or weighed in the usual manner, have no redemption, and may be brought from outside the Land even if blemished. Rabbi Shimon explains the rationale.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the substitute of a firstborn or tithe animal, and their offspring forever, have the same status and may be eaten by the owners if blemished.
The Mishnah lists the first difference: unlike other sacrifices, firstborn and tithe animals cannot be sold or weighed in the usual manner.
The Mishnah lists further differences: other sacrifices have redemption, but firstborn and tithe do not; and they may be brought from outside the Land, unlike others.
Rabbi Shimon explains the rationale: firstborn and tithe have a source of sustenance from their own place, whereas other sacrifices remain in their sanctity even if blemished.

items.text: Gemara: Question on blemishing a substitute of firstborn or tithe
items.text_en: Gemara: Question on blemishing a substitute of firstborn or tithe
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Azza raises a question from the West: is one who blemishes a substitute of a firstborn or tithe liable? Abaye challenges him to also ask about the ninth animal of the tithe. The Gemara explains that both are excluded by verses: the substitute is not offered, and the ninth is not the tenth.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Azza's question from the West
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Azza's question from the West
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Azza raises a question from the West: is one who blemishes a substitute of a firstborn or tithe liable, given that the substitute is not offered, or is he liable because it is consecrated?
Abaye challenges Rava bar Rav Azza to also ask about one who blemishes the ninth animal of the tithe, which is similarly excluded from sacrifice.
The Gemara explains that the ninth animal is excluded by the verse 'עֲשִׂירִי' (the tenth), which excludes the ninth, so the question about the ninth is not asked.

The Gemara resolves that the substitute of a firstborn or tithe is also excluded by the verse 'לֹא תִפְדֶּה קֹדֶשׁ הֵם' (they are holy), meaning they are offered but their substitute is not offered, so one who blemishes the substitute is not liable.

items.text: Alternative version of the question
items.text_en: Alternative version of the question
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak presents a different version: Rav Acha bar Rav Azza asked about the ninth animal of the tithe, and the response was to ask about the substitute of firstborn or tithe. Both are excluded by verses.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative version
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative version
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak presents an alternative version of the earlier discussion, where Rav Acha bar Rav Azza asked about the ninth animal of the tithe.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Azza's question
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Azza's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Azza asks in the West: what is the law for one who blemishes the ninth animal of the tithe?
The response redirects the question: why not ask about blemishing the substitute of a firstborn or tithe instead?

The gemara explains that both the substitute of firstborn/tithe and the ninth animal are excluded by verses: 'קֹדֶשׁ הֵם' (they are holy) excludes the substitute, and 'הָעֲשִׂירִי' (the tenth) excludes the ninth.

items.text: Contradiction regarding bringing firstborn from outside the Land
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding bringing firstborn from outside the Land
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says firstborn may be brought from outside the Land, but a baraita says Ben Antignos brought firstborn from Babylonia and they were not accepted. Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by attributing the views to Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says bekhor may be brought from outside the land, but Ben Antignos brought bekhorot from Babylonia and they were not accepted.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yishmael and the incident to Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on bringing tithe and firstborn
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on bringing tithe and firstborn
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei in the name of three elders: Rabbi Yishmael argues that one cannot bring second tithe in the present era, using a comparison to firstborn and first fruits. Rabbi Akiva counters with a verse that equates tithe to firstborn. The Gemara explains why a fortiori argument fails due to a common element involving the altar.

sub.text: Baraita citation (Rabbi Yosei quoting three elders)
sub.text_en: Baraita citation (Rabbi Yosei quoting three elders)
sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing Rabbi Yosei reporting three things in the name of three elders, and Rabbi Yishmael's question: can one bring second tithe in the present era and eat it in Jerusalem?

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael's a fortiori argument (first attempt)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's a fortiori argument (first attempt)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael attempts a הֶקֵּשׁ (analogy) from firstborn to tithe, then rejects it because the firstborn involves blood and altar-parts.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael's second a fortiori argument
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's second a fortiori argument
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael tries another a fortiori argument from first fruits to tithe, but is rejected because first fruits require a waving ceremony.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's rejoinder — Scriptural a fortiori proof
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's rejoinder — Scriptural a fortiori proof
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva counters by citing a Scriptural verse that explicitly connects tithe to firstborn, establishing that tithe must be eaten only within the Temple precinct boundaries through a הֶקֵּשׁ (textual analogy).

sub.text: Gemara's question on the logical argument
sub.text_en: Gemara's question on the logical argument
sub.desc_en: The gemara questions why Rabbi Akiva cannot simply use a standard a fortiori argument from the common side of firstborn and first fruits.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's answer — explaining the common element
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer — explaining the common element
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the a fortiori argument is invalid because both firstborn and first fruits share an altar element that the tithe lacks, breaking the common side comparison.

items.text: Analysis of the dispute regarding sanctity of the Land
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute regarding sanctity of the Land
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the underlying dispute: whether the original sanctity of the Land sanctified for the future. If it did, both firstborn and tithe may be brought; if not, even firstborn is questionable. The Gemara resolves that the case involves a firstborn whose blood was sprinkled before the Temple was destroyed, and its meat remains, but since the blood cannot be sprinkled now, the meat derives its status from the blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what underlying assumption Rabbi Yishmael holds regarding the sanctity of the Land, presenting two possibilities: if the original sanctity sanctified for the future, both firstborn and tithe may be brought; if not, even firstborn is questionable.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yishmael holds the original sanctity did not sanctify for the future, but the case involves a firstborn whose blood was sprinkled before the Temple was destroyed, and its meat remains; since the blood cannot be sprinkled now, the meat derives its status from the blood.

items.text: Gemara's question on learning ma'aser from bekhor
items.text_en: Gemara's question on learning ma'aser from bekhor
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether ma'aser can be derived from bekhor, citing Rabbi Yochanan's principle that in matters of kodashim one does not learn a 'lamed' from a 'lamed'. It then addresses the distinction between ma'aser being chullin and the different opinions on whether to follow the 'lamed' or the 'melamed'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether ma'aser can be derived from bekhor, citing Rabbi Yochanan's principle that in matters of kodashim one does not learn a 'lamed' from a 'lamed'.
The Gemara answers that ma'aser is chullin, and addresses the distinction between following the 'lamed' or the 'melamed', concluding that both are the same matter.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's teaching on bringing bekhor from outside the land
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's teaching on bringing bekhor from outside the land
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva teaches that one may only bring a bekhor from outside the land to the Temple when one can also bring ma'aser dagan, implying a geographical limitation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva teaches that one may only bring a bekhor from outside the land when one can also bring ma'aser dagan, implying a geographical limitation.
Rabbi Akiva concludes that from a place where one does not bring ma'aser dagan, one does not bring a bekhor.

items.text: Ben Azzai's argument on ma'aser sheni consumption
items.text_en: Ben Azzai's argument on ma'aser sheni consumption
items.desc_en: Ben Azzai argues that ma'aser sheni should be eaten only within the walls of Jerusalem, like bekhor, using a kal vachomer and a hekesh. The Gemara explains the underlying question about the difference between Shiloh and Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: Ben Azzai opens with a kal vachomer argument that ma'aser sheni should be eaten only within the walls of Jerusalem, like bekhor.
The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer is flawed because bekhor requires blood and sacrificial portions on the altar, which ma'aser sheni does not.
Ben Azzai counters with a hekesh (verbal analogy) from the verse, equating ma'aser sheni to bekhor for the rule of eating within the walls.

The Gemara asks what difficulty prompted Ben Azzai's opening 'יכול' (one might think), explaining the background about the difference between Shiloh and Jerusalem regarding where ma'aser sheni is eaten.
The Gemara resolves that Ben Azzai's statement teaches that even in Jerusalem, ma'aser sheni must be eaten within the walls, not anywhere in the city.

items.text: Acheirim's teaching on bekhor that passed its year
items.text_en: Acheirim's teaching on bekhor that passed its year
items.desc_en: Acheirim teaches that a bekhor that has passed its year is not invalidated, using a hekesh to ma'aser which is not invalidated from year to year.

sub.desc_en: Acheirim raises the possibility that a bekhor (firstborn animal) that has passed its year might be invalidated like other disqualified consecrated items.
Acheirim rejects the possibility by citing a verse that juxtaposes bekhor to ma'aser (tithe), concluding that just as ma'aser is not invalidated from year to year, so too bekhor is not invalidated.

items.text: Debate between Rabbanan and Acheirim on the source for bekhor not being invalidated
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbanan and Acheirim on the source for bekhor not being invalidated
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts the Rabbanan's derivation from the verse 'lifnei Hashem Elohecha tochlenu shanah beshanah' with Acheirim's use of the same verse to teach that bekhor is eaten for two days and one night. The Rabbanan derive the two-day eating period from the verse 'yihyeh lecha kachazeh hatenufah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For the Rabbanan, who derive a different law from the verse 'lifnei Hashem Elohecha tochlenu shanah beshanah', from where do they derive that a bekhor is not invalidated from one year to the next?
The Gemara answers: The Rabbanan derive it from the verse 'lifnei Hashem Elohecha tochlenu shanah beshanah', which teaches that the bekhor is not invalidated from one year to the next.
The Gemara asks: And for Acheirim, what do they derive from the verse 'lifnei Hashem Elohecha tochlenu shanah beshanah'?
The Gemara answers: Acheirim require it for the teaching of a baraita that one day from this year and one day from the next year teaches that the bekhor is eaten for two days and one night.
The Gemara asks: And for the Rabbanan, from where do they derive that the bekhor is eaten for two days and one night?
The Gemara answers: The verse states 'yihyeh lecha kachazeh hatenufah' (it shall be for you like the breast of the wave offering), teaching the two-day eating period.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter and opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter and opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The daf concludes the previous chapter and introduces the Mishnah listing cases where a chatat offering must die and does not effect temurah.

sub.text: Closing formula of the previous chapter
sub.text_en: Closing formula of the previous chapter
sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the previous chapter with the standard closing formula 'we return to you, these sacred offerings'.
The Mishnah lists cases where a chatat offering must die and does not effect temurah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sin-offering whose year has passed or that was lost and found blemished: if after atonement it dies, if before atonement it grazes until blemished, is sold, and another is brought with its proceeds; it can effect temurah and one is liable for me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of a sin-offering whose year passed or was lost and found blemished: after atonement it dies, before atonement it grazes until blemished, is sold, and another is brought with its proceeds; it can effect temurah and one is liable for me'ilah.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not teach the cases together, and explains that the first clause is absolute (the animal dies) while the second is conditional (it grazes). It then asks why the Mishnah teaches both me'ilah and temurah, and answers that it teaches temurah here, and because it taught temurah it also taught me'ilah, and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not teach the cases together, and explains that the first clause is absolute (the animal dies) while the second is conditional (it grazes).
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches temurah here, and because it taught temurah it also taught me'ilah, and vice versa.

items.text: Resh Lakish's statement
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's statement
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says: A sin-offering whose year has passed is considered as if it is standing in a cemetery, and it grazes (i.e., it is not left to die but is put out to pasture).

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that a sin-offering whose year has passed is treated as if it stands in a cemetery and is put out to pasture.

items.text: Challenge to Resh Lakish from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Resh Lakish from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Resh Lakish from the Mishnah: It teaches that if the year passed and it was lost and found blemished, after atonement it dies. This contradicts Resh Lakish who said it grazes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Resh Lakish by citing the Mishnah: if the year passed and it was lost and found blemished, after atonement it dies — contradicting Resh Lakish's ruling that it grazes.

items.text: Resh Lakish's defense and Rabbah's explanation
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's defense and Rabbah's explanation
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish responds that the Mishnah's 'dies' refers only to the case of lost and found blemished, not to the case of the year passing. The Gemara objects that if so, the clause 'if before atonement it grazes' is problematic for a blemished animal that is already blemished. Rabbah then explains that the Mishnah refers to a temporary blemish that will become permanent.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish responds that the Mishnah's 'dies' clause refers only to the case of lost and found blemished, not to the case of the year passing.
The Gemara objects that if so, the clause 'if before atonement it grazes' is problematic for a blemished animal that is already blemished.
Rabbah explains that the Mishnah refers to a temporary blemish that will become permanent.

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava raises two objections: if so, the Mishnah should have said 'it will be kept' (יִשְׁמוֹר), and why mention 'whose year passed'? Rava then explains that the Mishnah means: if the year passed and it was lost, or it was lost and found blemished – after atonement it dies, before atonement it grazes until blemished and is sold.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises two objections: if the Mishnah meant a temporary blemish, it should have said 'it will be kept' (יִשְׁמוֹר), and why mention the case of 'whose year passed' at all?
Rava explains that the Mishnah means: if the year passed and it was lost, or it was lost and found blemished – after atonement it dies, before atonement it grazes until blemished and is sold.

items.text: Need to teach both cases
items.text_en: Need to teach both cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah must teach the case of loss both for a blemished animal and for one whose year passed: each case has a unique reason why loss might be effective, and without both we might err.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah must teach the case of loss for a blemished animal: without it, one might think that loss is ineffective for a blemished animal that is otherwise fit for its purpose.

The Gemara adds that the case of a blemished animal alone would not suffice, because for an animal whose year passed, which is fit for sacrifice, one might think loss is ineffective; therefore both cases are necessary.

items.text: Rava's earlier statement on nighttime loss
items.text_en: Rava's earlier statement on nighttime loss
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's consistency: he previously said that loss at night is not considered loss. The Gemara distinguishes: nighttime loss is not fit for anything, but here the animal is fit for its monetary value even if not for sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's consistency, citing his earlier statement that loss at night (אבידה דלילה) is not considered loss.
The Gemara distinguishes: nighttime loss is not fit for anything, but here the animal is fit for its monetary value even if not for sacrifice.

items.text: Comparison with communal sin-offering and Rabbi Yochanan's principle
items.text_en: Comparison with communal sin-offering and Rabbi Yochanan's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that a second (communal sin-offering) grazes and its proceeds go to the Temple treasury, because a communal sin-offering does not die, implying an individual's does. Rabbi Yochanan says that living animals can be rejected, and one atones with the second of the pair. The Gemara explains that the first becomes like one whose year passed, and only because it is communal does it not die. The Gemara concludes that rejected animals are different from lost ones: lost ones might be found, rejected ones cannot return to fitness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that the second animal of a pair designated for a sin-offering grazes and its proceeds go to the Temple treasury, because a communal sin-offering does not die, implying that an individual's sin-offering does die.
Rabbi Yochanan states that living animals can be rejected (נדחין), and one atones with the second animal of the second pair.
The Gemara explains that the first animal becomes like one whose year passed (עיברה שנתה), and only because it is a communal offering does it not die; an individual's would die.
The Gemara concludes that rejected animals (דחויין) are different from lost ones (אבודין): lost ones might be found, but rejected ones cannot return to fitness.

items.text: Opening discussion: lost animal at night vs day
items.text_en: Opening discussion: lost animal at night vs day
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a lost animal at night is considered 'lost' (avudah). The debate aligns with Rabbi vs Rabbis: Rabbi holds that loss at night is not avudah, while Rabbis hold that even daytime loss is avudah if it occurs during the separation time. The Gemara clarifies that the dispute is about loss during the separation time, not about the animal's location.

items.text: Abaye's ruling: lost vs stolen
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling: lost vs stolen
items.desc_en: Abaye states: we hold that a lost animal (avudah) is not the same as a stolen one (genuvah), nor as a robbed one (gazulah). This sets the baseline for distinguishing types of loss.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yochanan define 'lost'
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yochanan define 'lost'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya defines 'lost' as even one animal in the herd or one in a group. Rabbi Yochanan says it is 'behind the door' (achorei hadalet). The Gemara questions whether 'behind the door' means where no one sees it, or where if one turns around they see it, and whether outside (abbarai) is also considered lost.

items.text: Rav Papa's question: lost in the cup
items.text_en: Rav Papa's question: lost in the cup
items.desc_en: Rav Papa asks: what is the status of blood lost in the cup (before sprinkling)? According to Rabbi, it is lost at the time of separation and thus dead. According to Rabbis, they might say it roams (ro'ah) before receiving the blood, but here they might consider it as already sprinkled (kezaruk dami).

items.text: Alternative view: lost at separation vs at sprinkling
items.text_en: Alternative view: lost at separation vs at sprinkling
items.desc_en: Some say the debate is always according to Rabbi, and the question is about a case where the blood was received in two cups and one was lost. According to the one who says a cup makes a vessel 'dachuy' (pushed aside), the question does not arise; according to the one who says a cup makes 'shiraim' (remnants), it does.

items.text: Mishna: separating sin-offering and losing it
items.text_en: Mishna: separating sin-offering and losing it
items.desc_en: The Mishna presents cases: one who separates a sin-offering and it is lost, then separates another; if the first is found later, both are valid — one is sacrificed, the other dies. If money for a sin-offering is lost and replaced, and the original money is found, the money goes to the Salt Sea. If one separates money for a sin-offering, loses it, separates other money, and before buying the offering the original is found — he brings from both, the remainder falls to donation.

items.text: Gemara on Mishna: why does the second die?
items.text_en: Gemara on Mishna: why does the second die?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why does the second sin-offering die if the first is found? It answers: according to the Rabbis, who say a lost animal at the time of separation roams (ro'ah) — so the second is not needed. But if the first was not lost at separation, it is valid and the second dies.

items.text: Mishna: separating money for sin-offering, lost, replaced, then found
items.text_en: Mishna: separating money for sin-offering, lost, replaced, then found
items.desc_en: The Mishna continues: if one separates money for a sin-offering, loses it, separates other money, and before buying the offering the original is found — he brings from both, the remainder falls to donation. The Gemara notes: the reason is that he brought from one of them, so the second goes to the Salt Sea. This aligns with Rabbi, who says lost at separation is dead.

items.text: Gemara resolves contradiction: first part Rabbis, second part Rabbi
items.text_en: Gemara resolves contradiction: first part Rabbis, second part Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the first part of the Mishna (about the sin-offering dying) follows Rabbis, but the second part (about money going to Salt Sea) follows Rabbi. Rav Huna explains: the first part is about a sin-offering that was lost at the time of separation (Rabbis), the second is about money lost before the offering was bought (Rabbi).

items.text: Introduction of the dispute: Rabbi Abba bar Rav's version
items.text_en: Introduction of the dispute: Rabbi Abba bar Rav's version
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a statement by Rabbi Abba bar Rav that all agree if one drew one animal and offered it, the second dies. The dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis is only when one seeks atonement with the lost animal: Rabbi considers the designation for loss as actual loss, while the Rabbis do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that all agree if one drew one animal and offered it, the second dies.

Rabbi Abba bar Rav explains that the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis is only when one seeks atonement with the lost animal: Rabbi considers the designation for loss as actual loss, while the Rabbis do not.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why repeat the dispute?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why repeat the dispute?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's first clause aligns with the Rabbis and the latter clause with Rabbi, questioning why the Mishnah teaches this dispute again. It answers that the Mishnah teaches that this matter is a dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara observes that the first clause of the Mishnah is taught anonymously in accordance with the Rabbis, and the latter clause in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to teach this dispute again, since it already explicitly states the disagreement between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis in the latter clause.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's explicit statement of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's position: one of the two sin offerings is sacrificed and the other dies.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah's explicit statement of the Rabbis' position: a sin offering dies only if found after atonement, and money goes to the Dead Sea only if found after atonement.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches that this matter is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis, clarifying the contradictory presentation.

items.text: Rav Huna's version of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Huna's version of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Huna cites Rav stating that all agree if one drew and offered one animal, the second dies. The dispute is only when one comes to consult: Rabbi holds no enactment was made for consecrated animals, so the lost animal dies; the Rabbis hold an enactment was made, so the non-lost animal grazes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna cites Rav stating that all agree if one drew and offered one animal, the second dies.

Rav Huna explains the dispute: when one consults, Rabbi holds no enactment was made for consecrated animals, so the lost animal dies; the Rabbis hold an enactment was made, so the non-lost animal grazes.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about eating on satiety
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about eating on satiety
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects: Was no enactment made for consecrated animals? A baraita teaches that if the eating is minimal, one adds hullin and terumah so it is eaten on satiety; if abundant, one does not add so it is not eaten on fullness. The Gemara clarifies this applies only to the Rabbis, not Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects to the claim that no enactment was made for consecrated animals, citing a baraita that teaches one adds hullin and terumah to a minimal meal so it is eaten on satiety.
The baraita continues: if the eating is abundant, one does not add hullin and terumah so it is not eaten on fullness.
The Gemara clarifies that the baraita applies only to the Rabbis, not to Rabbi.

items.text: Repetition of Rabbi Abba bar Rav's statement
items.text_en: Repetition of Rabbi Abba bar Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats Rabbi Abba bar Rav's statement that all agree if one atones with the non-lost animal, the lost one dies. The dispute is when one atones with the lost animal: Rabbi considers designation for loss as actual loss, the Rabbis do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara repeats Rabbi Abba bar Rav's statement that all agree if one atones with the non-lost animal, the lost one dies; the dispute is when one atones with the lost animal: Rabbi considers designation for loss as actual loss, the Rabbis do not.

items.text: Mishnah and Rav's ruling on communal vs. individual hatat
items.text_en: Mishnah and Rav's ruling on communal vs. individual hatat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the second animal of a pair grazes until blemished, is sold, and its proceeds go to a donation, because a communal hatat does not die. The Gemara infers that an individual's hatat does die. Rav explains that living animals are not rejected; when one atones with the second of the first pair, the other becomes like one designated for loss, and only because it is communal does it not die.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the second animal of a pair grazes until blemished, is sold, and its proceeds go to a donation, because a communal hatat does not die.
The Gemara infers that an individual's hatat does die, contrasting with the communal case.
Rav explains that living animals are not rejected; when one atones with the second of the first pair, the other becomes like one designated for loss, and only because it is communal does it not die.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's author
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's statement that a lost sin-offering that was replaced must die applies even according to the Rabbis, and concludes it is only according to Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that a lost sin-offering replaced by another must die applies even according to the Rabbis.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah reflects only Rabbi's opinion, not the Rabbis'.

items.text: Refutation of both opinions from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Refutation of both opinions from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: one who sets aside a sin-offering that was lost and then offers another in its place must die. The Gemara infers that only if he offered it does it die, otherwise it grazes, regardless of atonement or drawing. This refutes both Rabbi and the Rabbis. The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches only a definitive case, not an uncertain one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: one who sets aside a sin-offering that was lost and then offers another in its place must die.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that only if he offered the second animal does it die, otherwise it grazes, regardless of atonement or drawing.
The Gemara declares this a refutation of both Rabbi and the Rabbis.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah teaches only a definitive case, not an uncertain one.

items.text: Second refutation from money for a sin-offering
items.text_en: Second refutation from money for a sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another Mishnah: one who sets aside money for a sin-offering, loses it, and sets aside other money, then the original is found, he brings a sin-offering from both and the remainder goes to a donation. The Gemara infers that only if he atones from both does the remainder go to donation, but if from one, it goes to the Dead Sea. This again refutes both opinions, and the Gemara answers similarly that the Mishnah teaches only a definitive case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: one who sets aside money for a sin-offering, loses it, sets aside other money, then finds the original, brings a sin-offering from both, and the remainder goes to a donation.
The Gemara infers that only if he atones from both does the remainder go to donation, but if from one, it goes to the Dead Sea.

The Gemara argues that this refutes both opinions (Rabbi and Rabbis), since the Mishnah's ruling applies regardless of whether the atonement is from the lost animal or not, and regardless of whether he pulled the animal or not.
The Gemara answers similarly: the Mishnah teaches only a definitive case (where he atones from both), not an uncertain one (where he atones from one).

items.text: Rabbi Ammi's ruling and its alignment
items.text_en: Rabbi Ammi's ruling and its alignment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi says: one who sets aside two piles of money for backup, atones with one, and the second goes to donation. The Gemara asks whose opinion this follows. It cannot be Rabbi (obvious) or the Rabbis (a fortiori), so it must be Rabbi Shimon, who might lack the concept of donation. The Gemara teaches that Rabbi Shimon does have donation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi rules that one who sets aside two piles of money for backup atones with one, and the second goes to donation (נדבה).
The Gemara asks whose opinion this ruling follows.
The Gemara rejects that it follows Rabbi (יהודה הנשיא), because Rabbi's position on lost money is obvious, and he would certainly agree regarding backup money.
The Gemara rejects that it follows the Rabbis, because a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) shows that if they permit donation even for lost money, backup money is even more obvious.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Ammi's ruling is needed only according to Rabbi Shimon, who might lack the concept of donation (נדבה), and it teaches that he does have it.

items.text: Proof that Rabbi Shimon accepts donation
items.text_en: Proof that Rabbi Shimon accepts donation
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that Rabbi Shimon accepts donation from a baraita about thirteen shofar chests in the Temple, including six for donation. Rabbi Nehemiah (or Rabbi Shimon) objects based on the midrash of Yehoyada the Kohen, which teaches that leftover sin and guilt offerings are used for burnt offerings whose hides go to priests. This shows Rabbi Shimon has donation, but the Gemara suggests he might only have it in one order.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that Rabbi Shimon lacks donation (נדבה), asking how one could possibly say that.
The Gemara cites a baraita describing thirteen shofar chests in the Temple, including six designated for donation (נדבה).
The baraita explains that the six donation chests are for burnt offerings from leftover funds, whose hides do not go to the priests, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Nehemiah (or some say Rabbi Shimon) objects that this would nullify the midrash of Yehoyada the Kohen.
The Gemara cites the midrash of Yehoyada the Kohen, which teaches that leftover sin and guilt offerings are used for burnt offerings whose hides go to the priests.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon indeed has donation (נדבה), but suggests it might only apply in one order (סדר).

items.text: Rabbi Hoshaya's ruling on two chatat for achrayut and the debate over its alignment
items.text_en: Rabbi Hoshaya's ruling on two chatat for achrayut and the debate over its alignment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Hoshaya states that one who sets aside two chatat for backup is atoned with one, and the other grazes. The Gemara questions whose view this follows: not the Rabbis (who would not allow it for achrayut), not Rabbi Shimon (who says five chatat die), but rather Rabbi, who only permits death for ibbud but not achrayut.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Hoshaya rules that one who sets aside two chatat for backup is atoned with one, and the other grazes.
The Gemara asks whose view this follows, first considering the Rabbis and rejecting because they do not even allow ibbud, so achrayut is certainly not permitted.
The Gemara rejects alignment with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that five chatat die, not that one grazes.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Hoshaya follows Rabbi, who permits death only for ibbud but not for achrayut.

items.text: Mishnah on blemished chatat and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's ruling
items.text_en: Mishnah on blemished chatat and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's ruling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sets aside a blemished chatat sells it and brings another. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says if the second was offered before the first was slaughtered, the first dies. The Gemara initially thinks he agrees with Rabbi even for achrayut, but concludes he follows his father Rabbi Shimon (five chatat die).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sets aside a blemished chatat sells it and brings another, and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon rules that if the second was offered before the first was slaughtered, the first dies because atonement has already been achieved.
The Gemara initially assumes that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon agrees with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and extends the rule even to achrayut (a case of setting aside a replacement in advance).
The Gemara rejects the assumption and concludes that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon follows his father Rabbi Shimon's view that five chatat offerings die, not Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's.

items.text: Rav's challenge from the Mishnah on communal vs. individual chatat
items.text_en: Rav's challenge from the Mishnah on communal vs. individual chatat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says a communal chatat does not die, implying an individual's does. Rav, who holds that mitzvah is in the first, argues that when atoned with the second of the first pair, the first becomes achrayut, yet the Mishnah says it dies. This is consistent with Rav's view that the mitzvah is in the first.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a communal chatat does not die, implying an individual's chatat does die.
Rav challenges: since living animals are not rejected, when one is atoned with the second of the first pair, the first becomes achrayut, yet the Mishnah says an individual's chatat dies.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's challenge is consistent with his own view that the mitzvah is in the first animal.

items.text: Baraita of Rav Shimi bar Zeri on lost chatat at different times
items.text_en: Baraita of Rav Shimi bar Zeri on lost chatat at different times
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Zeri taught before Rav Pappa: If the chatat was lost at the time of designation, according to Rabbi it dies, according to the Rabbis it grazes. If lost at the time of atonement, according to the Rabbis it dies, according to Rabbi it grazes. The Gemara initially objects with a kal vachomer, then corrects the baraita: at the time of atonement, all agree it dies.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Zeri teaches before Rav Pappa a baraita about a lost chatat: if lost at designation time, according to Rabbi it dies, according to the Rabbis it grazes; if lost at atonement time, according to the Rabbis it dies, according to Rabbi it grazes.

The Gemara objects with a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if at designation time, where the Rabbis say it grazes, Rabbi says it dies, then at atonement time, where the Rabbis say it dies, Rabbi should certainly say it dies — contradicting the baraita's claim that Rabbi says it grazes.
The Gemara corrects the baraita: at designation time, Rabbi says it dies and the Rabbis say it grazes; at atonement time, all agree it dies.

items.text: Continuation of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.text_en: Continuation of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara references the continuation of the Mishnah with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's opinion, which will be discussed further.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara references the continuation of the Mishnah with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's opinion, which will be discussed further.

items.text: Baraita on not 'margilin' on Yom Tov, with bechor and disqualified sacrifices
items.text_en: Baraita on not 'margilin' on Yom Tov, with bechor and disqualified sacrifices
items.desc_en: A baraita states one does not 'margilin' on Yom Tov, nor with a bechor or disqualified sacrifices. The Gemara identifies the author for bechor as Beit Shammai (who hold bechor retains sanctity), and for disqualified sacrifices as Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon (who is stringent). The Gemara questions why not attribute both to one authority, and explains each authority's specific reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one does not 'margilin' (make a show of bringing) on Yom Tov, nor with a bechor (firstborn animal), nor with disqualified sacrifices.
The Gemara asks: granted the Yom Tov case is because of unnecessary exertion, but who is the Tanna of the bechor ruling?
Rav Chisda answers that the bechor ruling follows Beit Shammai, who hold that a bechor retains its sanctity and cannot be traded.
The Gemara asks who is the Tanna for the ruling on disqualified sacrifices.
Rav Chisda answers that the ruling on disqualified sacrifices follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who is stringent about such animals.
The Gemara objects: why not attribute both rulings (bechor and disqualified sacrifices) to Beit Shammai?
The Gemara rejects this: Beit Shammai's stringency applies only to a bechor, whose sanctity is from the womb, not to disqualified sacrifices.
The Gemara objects: why not attribute both rulings to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon?
The Gemara rejects this: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's stringency applies only to disqualified sacrifices, whose redemption is stringent, but not to a bechor.

items.text: Reconciling Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon with the Mishnah on selling disqualified sacrifices
items.text_en: Reconciling Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon with the Mishnah on selling disqualified sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Does Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon not accept the Mishnah that all disqualified sacrifices are sold in the market? This implies that once permitted, one may fatten and sell. Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana answers that what improves the skin damages the meat. In the West they say it appears as if one is working with consecrated animals. Rabbi Yosei bar Avin says it is a decree lest one raise herds from them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon rejects the Mishnah that all disqualified sacrifices may be slaughtered and sold in the market, implying that once permitted one may fatten and sell.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana answers that what improves the skin damages the meat, so fattening would not be beneficial.

sub.text: Western sages' answer in the name of Rabbi Avin
sub.text_en: Western sages' answer in the name of Rabbi Avin
sub.desc_en: In the West they say in the name of Rabbi Avin that it appears as if one is working with consecrated animals.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin says it is a decree lest one raise herds from them.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: How to circumvent the firstborn's sanctity
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: How to circumvent the firstborn's sanctity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a pregnant firstborn animal is designated: if the offspring is male, it is an olah; if female, a shelamim. It details outcomes for twins and concludes with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling that tumtum and androgynos do not become sanctified.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of circumventing the firstborn's sanctity by designating the offspring conditionally as an olah or shelamim.
The Mishnah details the outcomes for twins: a male and female, two males, or two females, with rules for selling the extra animal.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that sanctity does not take effect on a tumtum or androgynos.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Rav Yehuda's ruling vs. Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Rav Yehuda's ruling vs. Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda permits causing a blemish in a firstborn before it emerges into the air of the world. The Gemara objects from the Mishnah, which only allows designating the offspring as an olah, not as shelamim, implying one cannot nullify its sanctity.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that it is permitted to cause a blemish in a firstborn animal before it emerges into the air of the world.
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah, which only allows designating the offspring as an עולה (burnt-offering), not as שלמים (peace-offerings), implying one cannot nullify its sanctity.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's answer: Distinction between Temple era and present
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's answer: Distinction between Temple era and present
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda clarifies that his ruling applies only in the present era when the Temple is not standing and the animal is unfit for sacrifice, whereas the Mishnah deals with the time when the Temple exists.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda distinguishes his ruling, which applies only in the present era when the Temple is not standing and the animal is unfit for sacrifice, from the Mishnah's context when the Temple exists.

items.text: Gemara's concern and resolution: Preventing misuse
items.text_en: Gemara's concern and resolution: Preventing misuse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav Yehuda's ruling is necessary, suggesting a decree lest the animal's head emerge and one blemish it. It concludes that even so, this is preferable to coming to shearing and working with the animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav Yehuda's ruling is needed in the present era, suggesting a decree lest the animal's head emerge and one blemish it.
The Gemara resolves that even so, permitting blemishing is preferable to the risk of coming to shearing and working with the animal.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's case: Female as shelamim
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's case: Female as shelamim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how a female can be sanctified as a shelamim in the context of a firstborn, and explains that the Mishnah's latter clause refers to a non-firstborn animal (behemah shel hekdesh).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a female can be sanctified as a shelamim in the context of a firstborn, since a female firstborn cannot be consecrated as a shelamim.
The Gemara answers that the latter clause of the Mishnah refers to a non-firstborn animal (behemah shel hekdesh), not to a firstborn.

items.text: Gemara's question on twins: Why not revert to mother's sanctity?
items.text_en: Gemara's question on twins: Why not revert to mother's sanctity?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling on twin males: why should the second be sold for an olah rather than retaining the mother's firstborn sanctity? It answers that the latter clause deals with a non-firstborn animal (behemet chullin).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why, if the mother is a consecrated animal (בהמת הקדש), the second twin should not revert to the mother's firstborn sanctity instead of being sold for an olah.
The Gemara answers that the latter clause of the Mishnah deals with a non-firstborn animal (בהמת חולין), not a consecrated one.

items.text: Conclusion: Reference to tumtum and androgynos
items.text_en: Conclusion: Reference to tumtum and androgynos
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly notes the Mishnah's ruling on tumtum and androgynos, setting up further discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara briefly notes the Mishnah's ruling on tumtum and androgynos, setting up further discussion.

items.text: Gemara's deduction of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view
items.text_en: Gemara's deduction of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that offspring of consecrated animals are sanctified only upon birth (בהתייתן), not from the womb, because otherwise sanctity would already apply to them from their mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why sanctity does not take effect on the offspring of consecrated animals according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The Gemara explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that offspring of consecrated animals become sanctified only upon their birth (בהתייתן), not from the womb.

items.text: Tanna's view that offspring are sanctified from the womb
items.text_en: Tanna's view that offspring are sanctified from the womb
items.desc_en: A different Tanna holds that offspring of consecrated animals are sanctified from the womb, as derived from a baraita discussing the verse 'בכור לא יקדיש' and the word 'אך' which divides the law, indicating that only a firstborn cannot be consecrated, but other offspring can be consecrated in the womb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that presents the opposing view: another Tanna holds that offspring of consecrated animals are sanctified from their mother's womb.
The baraita begins by deriving from the verse 'בכור לא יקדיש' that a firstborn cannot be consecrated, but a person can consecrate a firstborn for other dedications.
The baraita continues: one might think others can consecrate it, but the verse 'בבהמה' limits the discussion to animals.
The baraita derives from 'אשר יבוכר לה׳' that one may consecrate a firstborn in the womb.
The baraita concludes that the word 'אך' divides the law, proving that offspring of all consecrated animals are sanctified from the womb.

items.text: Question about designating a firstborn as an olah during birth
items.text_en: Question about designating a firstborn as an olah during birth
items.desc_en: Rav Amram asks Rav Sheshet whether declaring a firstborn 'with the emergence of most of it – an olah' makes it an olah or a firstborn. Rav Sheshet compares this to a similar question of Ilfa about gleanings, and Abaye resolves it by noting that the words of the master (the Torah's law of firstborn) take precedence over the words of the student (the owner's declaration).

sub.text: Rav Amram's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Amram's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Amram asks Rav Sheshet whether declaring a firstborn 'with the emergence of most of it – an olah' makes it an olah or a firstborn.
The gemara presents an alternative version of the question: whether the sanctity of an olah applies to each part as it emerges, or the firstborn sanctity from the womb prevails.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet's comparison to Ilfa's question
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet's comparison to Ilfa's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet compares the question to Ilfa's similar dilemma about gleanings: whether declaring gleanings 'with the emergence of most of it – hefker' makes it hefker or gleanings.

Abaye resolves the question by invoking the principle that the words of the master (the Torah's law of firstborn) take precedence over the words of the student (the owner's declaration), so it remains a firstborn.

items.text: Mishnah: Designating mother and offspring with different sanctities
items.text_en: Mishnah: Designating mother and offspring with different sanctities
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where one declares the offspring as an olah and the mother as a shelamim, or vice versa. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei dispute the validity: Rabbi Meir holds that if the mother is first designated shelamim, the offspring becomes a shelamim; Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between initial intent and a change of mind.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one says 'her offspring is an elevation-offering and she is a peace-offering,' his words stand.
Rabbi Meir rules that if one says 'she is a peace-offering and her offspring is an elevation-offering,' the offspring is a peace-offering.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: if he intended both names from the start, his words stand; if he changed his mind after saying 'she is a peace-offering,' the offspring is a peace-offering.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a pregnant chatat
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a pregnant chatat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one designates a pregnant chatat and she gives birth, he may choose to be atoned by either the mother or the offspring, because the offspring is not considered a limb of the mother (עובר לאו ירך אמו), and the leftover sanctity applies to both as if he had set aside two chatats for liability.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that if one set aside a pregnant sin-offering and she gave birth, he may achieve atonement with either the mother or the offspring.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds the principle 'if he left a remainder, it is considered leftover' (שיירו משוייר), and the fetus is not considered a limb of its mother, so it is like setting aside two sin-offerings for backup.
The Gemara resolves that the fetus is not considered a limb of the mother (עובר לאו ירך אמו), so it is like designating two chatats for liability, and he may choose either.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Elazar and resolution by Rav Tavla
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Elazar and resolution by Rav Tavla
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar objects from the Mishnah that if the offspring were considered separate, the Mishnah should have said 'הרי זו שלמים' rather than 'הרי זה ולד שלמים'. Rav Tavla resolves that the Mishnah's text is indeed 'הרי זו שלמים', as Rav instructed the Tanna to teach.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar objects from the Mishnah: if the offspring were considered separate, the Mishnah should have taught 'הרי זו שלמים' (this is a peace-offering) rather than 'הרי זה ולד שלמים' (this is the offspring of a peace-offering).
Rav Tavla resolves that the Mishnah's text is indeed 'הרי זו שלמים', as Rav instructed the Tanna to teach that version.

items.text: Support from the case of a pregnant maidservant
items.text_en: Support from the case of a pregnant maidservant
items.desc_en: A baraita about a man telling his pregnant maidservant 'you are a maidservant and your child is free' is brought as support. If the offspring were not considered a limb, the child would be free, but here the maidservant acquires the child, implying the offspring is a limb, consistent with Rabbi Meir's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a man who tells his pregnant maidservant 'you are a maidservant and your child is free,' and the child is freed.
The Gemara explains that this baraita follows the view that 'if he left a remainder, it is not considered leftover,' and the fetus is a limb of its mother, and it aligns with Rabbi Meir's position.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who frees half his slave, the slave goes free, as the writ and the slave's hand come simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who frees half his slave, the slave goes free because the writ of emancipation and the slave's hand (to receive it) come simultaneously.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's view that the remaining portion is retained, using a baraita about a slave receiving a writ for another, and concludes that the remaining portion is not retained, refuting Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan: if the remaining portion is retained, why does the fetus acquire freedom through the slave's hand?
The Gemara cites a baraita that a slave can receive a writ of emancipation for another slave from a master who is not his own, implying the fetus cannot acquire through the mother's hand.
The Gemara concludes that the remaining portion is not retained, refuting Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and the Sages
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute is between Tannaim: Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds the remaining portion is not retained, while the Sages hold it is retained, citing the verse about the woman and her children.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute about whether the remaining portion is retained is a Tannaic dispute, citing the baraita where Rabbi Yose HaGelili and the Sages argue about a maidservant and her child.
The baraita presents the Sages' position that the man's words are upheld, citing the verse 'the woman and her children shall be her master's'.
