The Gemara asks what the verse teaches according to the Sages, and Rava explains that Rabbi Yose HaGelili interprets the verse to mean that when the mother belongs to the master, the child also belongs to the master.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute is indeed about whether the remaining portion is retained: Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds it is not retained, while the Sages hold it is retained.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's defense
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's defense
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that all agree the remaining portion is retained; the dispute is about the verse's interpretation regarding the woman and her children.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan responds that all agree the remaining portion is retained (שיירו משוייר), and the dispute is about the verse's interpretation regarding the woman and her children.

items.text: Second Tannaitic dispute: slaughtering a sin-offering with a live fetus
items.text_en: Second Tannaitic dispute: slaughtering a sin-offering with a live fetus
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another Tannaitic dispute about a sin-offering with a live four-day-old fetus, suggesting it hinges on whether the remaining portion is retained. Rabbi Yochanan explains it instead depends on when the offspring become sanctified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute about a sin-offering with a live four-day-old fetus is actually between Tannaim, citing one baraita that treats the animal as a full sin-offering.
A second baraita is cited, treating the same animal as a non-sacred animal, permitted to all people anywhere at any time.
The Gemara infers that the two baraitot disagree about whether the remaining portion (שיירו) is retained (משוייר) or not.

Rabbi Yochanan rejects the inference, asserting that all agree the remaining portion is retained; the dispute is about whether offspring of consecrated animals are sanctified at the moment of conception (במעי אמן) or only at birth (בהווייתן).

items.text: Alternative resolution: timing of consecration and pregnancy
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: timing of consecration and pregnancy
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: the two baraitot are not contradictory, as one case involves consecration before pregnancy, the other pregnancy before consecration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction between the two baraitot by distinguishing the timing: one case involves consecration before pregnancy, the other pregnancy before consecration.

items.text: Rava's objection and Rav Hamnuna's response
items.text_en: Rava's objection and Rav Hamnuna's response
items.desc_en: Rava objects that Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning might be that a person achieves atonement through the improvement of consecrated property. Rav Hamnuna dismisses this, noting that Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yochanan's student, did not accept this explanation.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning might not be that leftover consecrated property is retained (שיירו משוייר), but rather that a person achieves atonement through the improvement (שבח) of consecrated property.
Rav Hamnuna rejects Rava's objection, noting that Rabbi Elazar, a close student of Rabbi Yochanan, did not accept this explanation, implying it is not Rabbi Yochanan's actual reasoning.

items.text: Discussion on retraction within speech
items.text_en: Discussion on retraction within speech
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where one says 'this is a peace-offering' and then retracts, clarifying that retraction is valid only within the time of speech, and Rav Pappa explains the need for this ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks a simple question: if one said 'this is a peace-offering' and then reconsidered, obviously the offspring are peace-offerings, so why is the case taught? When can one retract?

Rav Pappa explains that the ruling is needed for a case where one retracts within תוך כדי דיבור (the time of speech), teaching that even though one might think retraction within that time is valid, here it is not because the person was merely reconsidering.

items.text: Mishnah: conflicting designations of temurah
items.text_en: Mishnah: conflicting designations of temurah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one says 'this is a substitute for a burnt-offering, a substitute for a peace-offering,' with Rabbi Meir ruling it is a substitute for a burnt-offering, and Rabbi Yose distinguishing between initial intent and retraction.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of one who says 'this is a substitute for a burnt-offering, a substitute for a peace-offering,' and Rabbi Meir rules it is a substitute for a burnt-offering.

Rabbi Yose distinguishes: if he intended both from the outset, his words stand because it is impossible to say two names simultaneously; but if he reconsidered after saying 'substitute of a burnt-offering,' it remains a substitute for a burnt-offering.

items.text: Gemara's opening analysis of the Mishnah's dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's opening analysis of the Mishnah's dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosei quotes Rabbi Yochanan stating that all agree when one says 'let this take effect' twice sequentially, the first expression is binding; when one says 'let this not take effect unless that takes effect', both are consecrated. The dispute in the Mishnah is only where one says 'temurat olah temurat shelamim', with Rabbi Meir treating it like sequential statements and Rabbi Yosei arguing that the phrasing teaches that the animal is consecrated but not offered.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosei quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosei quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosei quotes Rabbi Yochanan stating that when one says 'let this take effect' twice sequentially, the first expression is binding, and when one says 'let this not take effect unless that takes effect', both are consecrated.
The Gemara clarifies that the dispute in the Mishnah is only in the case where one says 'temurat olah temurat shelamim'.
Rabbi Meir treats the phrasing as if the speaker said 'let this take effect and afterwards let this take effect', so the first expression is binding.
Rabbi Yosei argues that the phrasing teaches that the animal is consecrated but not offered, unlike if he had said 'temurat olah ushelamim'.

items.text: Baraita on half-consecration as a substitute for olah and shelamim
items.text_en: Baraita on half-consecration as a substitute for olah and shelamim
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if one says 'this animal half is temurat olah and half temurat shelamim', Rabbi Meir says it is entirely offered as olah, while the Sages say it grazes until blemished and is sold, with proceeds used for both offerings. Rabbi Yosei says if he intended from the start, since it's impossible to utter two names simultaneously, his words stand. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yosei's view is identical to the Sages, and the entire baraita is taught according to Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the case of half-consecration as a substitute for olah and shelamim, and records Rabbi Meir's ruling that the entire animal is offered as olah.
The Sages rule that the animal grazes until blemished, is sold, and the proceeds are used for both olah and shelamim offerings.
Rabbi Yosei rules that if the person intended from the start, since it is impossible to utter two names simultaneously, his words stand.
The Gemara asks: Rabbi Yosei's ruling is identical to the Sages — why is it stated separately?
The Gemara resolves that the entire baraita is taught according to Rabbi Yosei's view, so the Sages' position is actually Rabbi Yosei's own.

items.text: Baraita on half-consecration as olah and chatat
items.text_en: Baraita on half-consecration as olah and chatat
items.desc_en: Another baraita: if one says 'half olah and half chatat', Rabbi Meir says it is entirely offered as olah; Rabbi Yosei says it must die. They agree that if one says 'half chatat and half olah', it must die. The Gemara asks who 'they agree' refers to—Rabbi Meir—and clarifies that without this teaching, one might think Rabbi Meir's reason is not 'we follow the first expression' but that a mixed chatat is offered; the baraita teaches that even when 'half chatat' is said first, it is not offered.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a case where one says 'half olah and half chatat': Rabbi Meir rules it is entirely offered as olah, while Rabbi Yosei rules it must die.
The baraita adds that both agree when one says 'half chatat and half olah' first, the animal must die.
The Gemara asks: 'They agree' — who does this refer to? It answers: Rabbi Meir, and notes this is obvious.
The Gemara explains that without this teaching, one might think Rabbi Meir's reason is not 'we follow the first expression' but that a mixed chatat is offered.
The baraita teaches that even when 'half chatat' is said first, it is not offered, confirming Rabbi Meir's principle of תפוס לשון ראשון (we follow the first expression).

items.text: Baraita on half-consecration as olah and shelamim with temurah
items.text_en: Baraita on half-consecration as olah and shelamim with temurah
items.desc_en: Another baraita: if one says 'this animal half olah and half shelamim', it is consecrated but not offered, it can effect temurah, and its temurah is like itself. The Gemara identifies this as Rabbi Yosei's view, noting that the novelty is about the temurah: one might think the temurah could be offered, but it teaches that since the original has a rejected sanctity, the temurah derived from it also cannot be offered.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that an animal designated half as an olah and half as shelamim is consecrated but not offered, can effect temurah, and its temurah is like itself.
The Gemara asks whose view this baraita follows, and notes that the rule of 'consecrated but not offered' is already obvious from Rabbi Yosei's position.

The Gemara explains that the baraita's novelty is about the temurah: one might think the temurah could be offered, but it teaches that since the original has a rejected sanctity (קדושה דחויה), the temurah derived from it also cannot be offered.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a partner's animal
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a partner's animal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules: if an animal belongs to two partners, and one consecrates his half, then later buys the other half and consecrates it, the animal is consecrated but not offered, can effect temurah, and its temurah is like itself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that an animal belonging to two partners, where one consecrates his half and later buys and consecrates the other half, is consecrated but not offered, can effect temurah, and its temurah is like itself.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers three principles from the Mishnah's case of 'like it' (כיוצא בה): that sanctity of value can be overridden, that living blemished animals are overridden, and that rejection from the outset is considered rejection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'like it' (כיוצא בה) that sanctity of value can be overridden.
The Gemara further infers that living blemished animals are overridden, and that rejection from the outset is considered rejection.

items.text: Abaye's query on mixed declarations
items.text_en: Abaye's query on mixed declarations
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that all agree when one says 'half for olah and half for ma'aser', the olah is offered. He then asks about 'half temurah and half ma'aser': does the temurah take precedence because it applies to all consecrated items, or does the ma'aser because it sanctifies before and after? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that everyone agrees when one says 'half of it is an olah and half is maaser', the olah is offered.
Abaye asks what the law is when one says 'half of it is a temurah and half is maaser'.

The Gemara presents the unresolved dilemma: whether the temurah is offered because it applies to all consecrated animals, or the maaser is offered because it can be consecrated before and after, and concludes with 'תיקו' (let it stand).

items.text: Mishnah: Language of substitution
items.text_en: Mishnah: Language of substitution
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that saying 'this is under this', 'this is the temurah of this', or 'this is the exchange of this' effects temurah, but 'this is redeemed onto this' does not. If the consecrated animal was blemished, it goes out to non-sacred status and requires payment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that saying 'this is under this', 'this is a temurah of this', or 'this is a replacement of this' effects temurah, but 'this is redeemed onto this' does not, and if the consecrated animal is blemished it goes out to non-sacred use and requires valuation.
The Mishnah adds that if the consecrated animal was blemished, it goes out to non-sacred status and requires payment.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction from bedek habayit
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction from bedek habayit
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'under' (תחת) is a language of substitution, citing a baraita on bedek habayit where 'exchange' or 'temurah' accomplishes nothing, but 'under' or 'redeemed onto' is effective. If 'under' implies substitution, why the difference between the cases?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'תחת' (under) is a language of substitution, citing a baraita about consecrated property of the Temple where 'חליפת זו' and 'תמורת זו' have no effect, but 'תחת זו' and 'מחוללת על זו' are valid.
The Gemara objects: if 'תחת' is a language of substitution, why is the first clause different from the second clause in the baraita?
Abaye answers that 'תחת' can be found as a language of substitution and as a language of desacralization, citing a verse.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: 'Under' is ambiguous
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: 'Under' is ambiguous
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the word 'under' (תחת) can be used both for substitution (as in the verse) and for redemption. Thus the Mishnah and baraita are consistent: context determines the meaning.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the word 'תחת' (under) can be used both for substitution (תפוסי) and for redemption (אחולי), depending on context.

items.text: Opening Gemara: The dual meaning of "תַּחַת"
items.text_en: Opening Gemara: The dual meaning of "תַּחַת"
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the word "תַּחַת" can mean either substitution (אַתְפּוֹסֵי) or desacralization (אַחוֹלֵי), citing a verse from Isaiah. It concludes that for sacrifices offered on the altar, which are subject to temurah, "תַּחַת" implies substitution; for items consecrated for Temple upkeep, which are not subject to temurah, it implies desacralization.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a verse (Leviticus 13:28) and explains that the word 'תַּחַת' can mean either substitution (אַתְפּוֹסֵי) or desacralization (אַחוֹלֵי), concluding that for altar sacrifices it implies substitution, for Temple upkeep items it implies desacralization.
Rava objects that even with altar sacrifices, one can find the desacralization meaning, such as when the consecrated animal has a blemish.

Rabbi Ashi resolves that even with a blemished animal, both meanings are possible: if the speaker's hand is on the consecrated animal, it becomes profane; if on the profane animal, it becomes consecrated.

items.text: Rava and Rav Ashi: Even in altar sacrifices, context matters
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Ashi: Even in altar sacrifices, context matters
items.desc_en: Rava argues that even in the case of altar sacrifices, if the consecrated animal is blemished, "תַּחַת" can mean desacralization. Rav Ashi adds that even with a blemished animal, the meaning depends on the speaker's intent: if his hand is on the consecrated animal, it becomes profane; if on the profane animal, it becomes consecrated.

sub.desc_en: Rava argues that even in the case of altar sacrifices (קדשי מזבח), one can find a context where "תַּחַת" means desacralization, such as when the consecrated animal is blemished.

Rav Ashi adds that even with a blemished animal, the meaning depends on the speaker's intent: if his hand is on the consecrated animal, it becomes profane; if on the profane animal, it becomes consecrated.

items.text: Abaye's first query: Two blemished consecrated animals and two unblemished profane animals
items.text_en: Abaye's first query: Two blemished consecrated animals and two unblemished profane animals
items.desc_en: Abaye asks: if one has two blemished consecrated animals and two unblemished profane animals, and says "these are under those," does he intend substitution (and is liable) or desacralization, since he could avoid sin by using the unblemished profane animals for substitution?

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks: if one has two blemished consecrated animals and two unblemished profane animals and says 'these are in place of those,' does he intend substitution (and is liable) or desacralization (since a person does not leave permitted for forbidden)?

The Gemara elaborates: does he intend substitution and incur lashes, or since there is a permissible path (using the unblemished profane animals for substitution) he would not abandon the permissible and commit a transgression, so he intends desacralization?

items.text: Abaye's second query: Mixed blemished and unblemished animals
items.text_en: Abaye's second query: Mixed blemished and unblemished animals
items.desc_en: Abaye asks: if one has two consecrated animals (one blemished) and two profane animals (one blemished), and says "these are under those," does he intend substitution for unblemished under unblemished and desacralization for blemished under blemished, or does he intend substitution for the profane unblemished under the consecrated blemished and the profane blemished under the consecrated unblemished, incurring liability for both?

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks a second case: if one has two consecrated animals (one blemished) and two profane animals (one blemished), does he pair perfect with perfect for substitution and blemished with blemished for desacralization, or does he pair each profane with a consecrated animal, making him liable for two lashes?

items.text: Abaye's third query: Three consecrated animals (one blemished) and three unblemished profane animals
items.text_en: Abaye's third query: Three consecrated animals (one blemished) and three unblemished profane animals
items.desc_en: Abaye asks: if one has three consecrated animals (one blemished) and three unblemished profane animals, and says "these are under those," do we say that since the unblemished profane animals are placed under the unblemished consecrated ones for substitution, the unblemished profane animals under the blemished consecrated one are also for substitution? Or do we say that the last one is for desacralization?

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks a third case: if one has three consecrated animals (one blemished) and three perfect profane animals, does he pair perfect with perfect for substitution, and also perfect with blemished for substitution, or does he avoid prohibition and the last pairing is for desacralization?

items.text: Rav Ashi's query: Four consecrated animals (one blemished) and four profane animals
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's query: Four consecrated animals (one blemished) and four profane animals
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks: if one has four consecrated animals (one blemished) and four profane animals, and says "these are under those," since the person is now established as a sinner (having performed substitution with the first three), does he incur four lashes, or does he still avoid sin and the last one is for desacralization? The question remains unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks: if one has four consecrated animals (one blemished) and four profane animals, does he definitely intend substitution for all four (since he is already established in transgression) and is liable for four lashes, or does he still avoid prohibition and the last pairing is for desacralization? The question remains unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).
The Gemara suggests: since the person is now established as a sinner (having performed substitution with the first three), he incurs four lashes.
The Gemara alternatively suggests: even though he is established in sin, he still avoids sin and the last animal is for desacralization, leaving the question unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

items.text: Mishnah and dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Mishnah and dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if consecrated property was blemished, it goes out to profane use. Rabbi Yochanan says it goes out by Torah law but requires valuation by rabbinic decree; Reish Lakish says valuation is also required by Torah law. The Gemara questions whether this applies to overcharging (אוֹנָאָה) or to voiding a sale (בִּטּוּל מִקָּח), concluding it must be about voiding a sale.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a consecrated animal was blemished, it goes out to profane use.
Rabbi Yochanan says the desacralization is by Torah law, but valuation is required by rabbinic decree.
Reish Lakish argues that even the requirement of valuation is by Torah law.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute concerns the case of exploitation (אוֹנָאָה).
The Gemara objects that consecrated property is not subject to the laws of exploitation, citing a Mishnah.
The Gemara concludes that the dispute must be about voiding a sale (בִּטּוּל מִקָּח), not exploitation.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yirmeyah and Rabbi Yonah on bittul mekach for hekdesh
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yirmeyah and Rabbi Yonah on bittul mekach for hekdesh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah and Rabbi Yonah both cite Rabbi Yochanan that ona'ah does not apply to hekdesh or land, but bittul mekach does. The Gemara questions whether the statement applies to bittul mekach or ona'ah, and Rabbi Yirmeyah concludes not to reverse the interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yirmeyah and Rabbi Yonah who both quote Rabbi Yochanan that the laws of אונאה (overreaching) do not apply to hekdesh or land, but ביטול מקח (annulment of the sale) does apply.
The Gemara questions whether the statement should be interpreted as referring to ביטול מקח (annulment of sale) and suggests reversing the attribution.
The Gemara objects that reversing the attribution works only for Rabbi Yonah who spoke about hekdesh, but not for Rabbi Yirmeyah who spoke about land.
The Gemara asks how one could reverse the statement for Rabbi Yirmeyah, who said the statement applies to land but not to hekdesh.
Rabbi Yirmeyah concludes that the attribution should not be reversed.

items.text: Attributing the dispute to Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Attributing the dispute to Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute is about Shmuel's ruling that hekdesh worth a maneh can be redeemed for a perutah. Rabbi Yonah rejects this, while Rabbi Yirmeyah accepts it. The Gemara refines: both accept Shmuel, but differ on whether it applies lechatchilah (ab initio).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yirmeyah revolves around Shmuel's ruling that hekdesh worth a maneh can be redeemed for a perutah.
The Gemara refines that both Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Yirmeyah accept Shmuel's ruling, but they disagree on whether it applies לכתחילה (ab initio) or only בדיעבד (after the fact).

items.text: Alternative resolution via Rav Chisda's explanation
items.text_en: Alternative resolution via Rav Chisda's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: do not reverse the interpretation, and resolve the difficulty with the Mishnah by Rav Chisda's teaching that 'no ona'ah' means even less than the standard overcharge voids the sale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: do not reverse the interpretation, and resolve the difficulty with the Mishnah by Rav Chisda's teaching that 'no ona'ah' means even less than the standard overcharge voids the sale.

items.text: Ulla's ruling on appraisal by three
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling on appraisal by three
items.desc_en: Ulla states that the leniency of bittul mekach applies only when appraised by two, but not by three. The Gemara questions this based on Rav Safra's principle, and explains that Ulla holds the appraisal is rabbinic, and the Sages were lenient.

sub.desc_en: Ulla rules that the leniency of bittul mekach applies only when appraised by two, but not by three, even if the price was off by a hundred.
The Gemara objects based on Rav Safra's principle that for appraisal we follow opinions, not numbers, so three should be more authoritative.
The Gemara further objects that if three appraisers disagree, we follow the later ones, and the principle of 'the hand of hekdesh is on the upper side' should apply.
Ulla holds that the appraisal is only rabbinic (מדבריהם), and the Sages were lenient in rabbinic matters.

items.text: Mishnah: Substitution formulas for sacrifices
items.text_en: Mishnah: Substitution formulas for sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that saying 'this is under an olah' or 'under a chatat' without specification accomplishes nothing. If one specifies 'under this olah' or 'under a chatat I have at home', it is valid. For a non-kosher or blemished animal, saying 'these are olah' does nothing, but 'these are for olah' requires sale and purchase of an olah with the proceeds.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that saying 'this is under an olah' or 'under a chatat' without specification accomplishes nothing.
The Mishnah rules that specifying 'under this chatat' or 'under this olah' or 'under a chatat or olah I have at home' is valid if he has such a sacrifice.
The Mishnah states that for a non-kosher or blemished animal, saying 'these are olah' accomplishes nothing.
The Mishnah concludes that saying 'these are for olah' requires sale and purchase of an olah with the proceeds.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav says the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Meir, who holds that one does not utter words in vain. Another statement: the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Shimon, who allows selling a blemished animal without a blemish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav states that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Meir, who holds that one does not utter words in vain.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling requiring a blemish for selling an animal designated for a sacrifice applies only to an unfit animal, but a female designated for an עולה (burnt offering) or אשם (guilt offering) requires a blemish to be sold.
Rav Yehudah citing Rav adds that the Mishnah also does not follow Rabbi Shimon, who permits selling a blemished animal without a blemish.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists animals forbidden for the altar that nullify mixtures in any amount: rove'a, nirba, mukshe, ne'evad, etnan, mechir, kil'ayim, treifah, and yotzei dofen. It then defines mukshe and ne'evad, noting that both are permitted for eating.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists animals forbidden for the altar that nullify mixtures in any amount.
The Mishnah defines mukshe and ne'evad, noting that both are permitted for eating.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on 'ossrin b'chol shehen'
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on 'ossrin b'chol shehen'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'ossrin b'chol shehen' means they are not nullified by a majority. It cites a baraita about kodashim mixed with chatat metah or shor haniskal, and clarifies that the baraita teaches that even though these are not prohibited for benefit, they still do not nullify.

sub.desc_en: Mar explains that 'ossrin b'chol shehen' means these items are not nullified by a majority (רוב).
A baraita is cited: all consecrated animals that become mixed with chatat metah or shor haniskal, even one in ten thousand, must die.
The Gemara asks: what is the baraita saying? (It seems redundant.)
The Gemara clarifies the baraita: it means that if consecrated animals became mixed with chatat metah or shor haniskal, even one in ten thousand, they must die.

The Gemara explains the necessity: one might have thought that since these are not prohibited for benefit (איסורי הנאה), they should be nullified by a majority, so the baraita teaches that they are not.

items.text: Comparison with rove'a and nirba in chullin and kodashim
items.text_en: Comparison with rove'a and nirba in chullin and kodashim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a baraita teaches that rove'a and nirba mixed with others must graze until blemished and then be sold. Rav Kahana reports that Rav Shimi bar Ashi distinguished between chullin and kodashim. The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: kodashim are repulsive, but chullin might be nullified; and chullin are not a prohibited benefit, but kodashim might be nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that teaches that a rove'a or nirba that became mixed with other animals must graze until blemished and then be sold, with the proceeds used to bring an offering of the finest type.

sub.text: Rav Kahana reporting Rav Shimi bar Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana reporting Rav Shimi bar Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports that Rav Shimi bar Ashi explained that one baraita deals with חולין (non-sacred animals) and the other with קדשים (sacred animals), resolving the apparent contradiction.

The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: regarding קדשים (sacred animals) the rule is needed because they are repulsive, but regarding חולין (non-sacred animals) one might think they should be nullified by a majority.
The Gemara cites another baraita listing items forbidden in חולין (non-sacred contexts) that also prohibit mixtures in any amount, including rove'a and nirba.

The Gemara explains that both baraitot are necessary: the first (קדשים) teaches about repulsiveness, the second (חולין) teaches about prohibition of benefit, and each alone would leave a gap for the other case.

items.text: Derivation that rove'a and nirba are forbidden for the altar
items.text_en: Derivation that rove'a and nirba are forbidden for the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source that rove'a and nirba are forbidden for the altar. It cites a brayta that derives from 'min habehemah' to exclude them. A logical argument from ba'al mum is refuted by choresh b'shor vachamor, and then by the lack of death penalty. Rabbi Shimon attempts a kal vachomer from ba'al mum regarding testimony, but the Gemara concludes that the verse is necessary because the logical derivation fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a rove'a (an animal that mounted a human) and a nirba (an animal that was mounted by a human) are forbidden for the altar?
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'min habehemah' (from the animal) to exclude rove'a and nirba from the altar.

The Gemara objects with a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if a ba'al mum (blemished animal), which has no sin, is disqualified from the altar, then rove'a and nirba, which have been used for sin, should certainly be forbidden.
The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer by citing choresh b'shor vachamor (plowing with an ox and a donkey), which involves a sin but is permitted for the altar.
The Gemara objects that choresh b'shor vachamor is not subject to the death penalty, unlike rove'a and nirba, which are.
The Gemara rejects this by noting that the death penalty applies only when the sin is witnessed by two valid witnesses, leaving a gap for cases without such testimony.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that rove'a and nirba are forbidden when the sin is established by a single witness or by the owner's own admission?

Rabbi Shimon attempts a kal vachomer: if a ba'al mum, which is not disqualified from eating by the testimony of two witnesses, is disqualified from sacrifice by a single witness's admission, then rove'a and nirba, which are disqualified from eating by two witnesses, should certainly be disqualified from sacrifice by a single witness's admission.
The Gemara concludes that the verse 'min habehemah' is necessary to exclude rove'a and nirba, because the logical derivation (kal vachomer) fails.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and resolution for rove'a and nirva
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and resolution for rove'a and nirva
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a potential objection: one might argue that a ba'al mum is disqualified because its blemish is visible, but a rove'a or nirva has no visible blemish and should be fit. The verse 'min habehemah' excludes them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a potential objection: one might argue that a ba'al mum is disqualified because its blemish is visible, but a rove'a or nirva has no visible blemish and should be fit.
Rav Ashi resolves the objection by citing the verse 'min habehemah' to exclude rove'a and nirva.

items.text: Derivation of ne'evad from 'min habakar' and the objection of nullifying the prohibition of idolatry
items.text_en: Derivation of ne'evad from 'min habakar' and the objection of nullifying the prohibition of idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that a ne'evad (animal worshipped) is excluded from 'min habakar'. It presents a kal vachomer from etnan and mechir, and an objection that this would nullify the prohibition of taking their silver and gold. The Gemara resolves that the verse applies only to inanimate objects, but for a living animal, the exclusion is needed.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the phrase 'from the herd' excludes an animal that was worshipped.
The Gemara asks why a verse is needed, proposing a kal vachomer (a fortiori inference) from etnan and mechir to prohibit a ne'evad.
An objection is raised by reversing the kal vachomer: if etnan and mechir are stringent yet their coating is permitted, then a ne'evad, which is lenient, should have its coating permitted.
The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that it would nullify the verse prohibiting taking silver and gold from idols.
The Gemara resolves that the verse applies only to inanimate objects, but for a living animal, the exclusion 'from the herd' is needed to prohibit its coating.

items.text: Rav Chananya's objection regarding the prohibition of idolatrous vessels
items.text_en: Rav Chananya's objection regarding the prohibition of idolatrous vessels
items.desc_en: Rav Chananya objects: if not for the verse, would the plating of a ne'evad be permitted? But the verse 've'ibadtem et shemam' prohibits anything made for their name. The Gemara explains that verse is for giving them derogatory names.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chananya objects: if not for the verse, would the plating of a ne'evad be permitted? But the verse 'וְאִבַּדְתֶּם אֶת שְׁמָם' (and you shall destroy their name) prohibits anything made for their name.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וְאִבַּדְתֶּם אֶת שְׁמָם' (and you shall destroy their name) is for giving them derogatory names, not for prohibiting their plating.

items.text: Attempt to reverse the exclusions and the contextual proof
items.text_en: Attempt to reverse the exclusions and the contextual proof
items.desc_en: One might suggest reversing the exclusions: 'min habehemah' for ne'evad and 'min habakar' for rove'a and nirva. The Gemara rejects this based on context: 'behemah' is associated with bestiality, 'bakar' with the golden calf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes reversing the exclusions: 'min habehemah' for ne'evad and 'min habakar' for rove'a and nirva.
The Gemara rejects the reversal based on contextual clues: 'behemah' is associated with bestiality, 'bakar' with the golden calf.

items.text: Exclusion of muktzah and noge'ach, and Rabbi Shimon's reasoning for both
items.text_en: Exclusion of muktzah and noge'ach, and Rabbi Shimon's reasoning for both
items.desc_en: The verses exclude muktzah (set aside for idolatry) and noge'ach (goring ox). Rabbi Shimon explains why both are needed: rove'a involves coercion like willingness, which noge'ach does not; noge'ach pays kofer, which rove'a does not.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the verse 'from the flock' excludes muktzah (set aside for idolatry) and 'and from the flock' excludes noge'ach (a goring ox).
Rabbi Shimon asks why both rove'a (one who copulates with an animal) and noge'ach are separately excluded, since one might seem redundant.
Rabbi Shimon explains that each exclusion is needed: rove'a involves coercion like willingness, which noge'ach does not; noge'ach pays kofer (ransom), which rove'a does not.

items.text: Baraita on rove'a and nirva requiring a permanent blemish, and the derivation from 'mushchatam'
items.text_en: Baraita on rove'a and nirva requiring a permanent blemish, and the derivation from 'mushchatam'
items.desc_en: A baraita states that rove'a and nirva are like consecrated animals that had a temporary blemish before consecration, requiring a permanent blemish for redemption. The verse 'ki mashchatam bahem mum bam' teaches this, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael interprets 'hashchata' as referring to sexual transgression or idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the case of rove'a and nirva, comparing them to consecrated animals that had a temporary blemish before consecration.
The baraita states that these animals require a permanent blemish for redemption, citing the verse 'כִּי מׇשְׁחָתָם בָּהֶם מוּם בָּם'.
The Gemara questions the baraita's wording, suggesting it is missing a clause about the prohibition of these animals.

The Gemara explains that the baraita should be read as teaching the prohibition from the verse, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael interprets 'hashchata' as referring to sexual transgression or idolatry.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael provides scriptural support for the interpretation of 'hashchata' as sexual transgression and idolatry, concluding that wherever a blemish disqualifies, these also disqualify.

items.text: Dispute between the Tanna and Beit Rabbi Yishmael on the derivation of choleh, zaken, and mezoham
items.text_en: Dispute between the Tanna and Beit Rabbi Yishmael on the derivation of choleh, zaken, and mezoham
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael uses the verses 'min habehemah, min habakar, umin hatzon' to exclude choleh (sick), zaken (old), and mezoham (disgusting). The first Tanna derives these from 'min hatzon, min hakevasim, umin ha'izim'. The school of Rabbi Yishmael holds that the verse speaks in its usual manner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verses 'min habehemah, min habakar, umin hatzon'.
The answer states that the school of Rabbi Yishmael needs these verses to exclude a sick, old, or disgusting animal.
The Gemara asks from where the first Tanna, who used these verses for rove'a and nirba, derives the exclusion of a sick, old, or disgusting animal.
The answer explains that the first Tanna derives these exclusions from the verses 'min hatzon, min hakevasim, umin ha'izim'.
The Gemara resolves that for the school of Rabbi Yishmael, the verse speaks in its usual manner, so they do not derive additional exclusions from those words.

items.text: Resh Lakish's definition of muktzah and the discussion of the night of Gideon
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's definition of muktzah and the discussion of the night of Gideon
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that only an animal set aside for seven years is forbidden as muktzah, citing the verse about Gideon's bull. The Gemara questions whether that bull was also ne'evad. Rav Acha bar Yaakov says it was set aside but not worshipped; Rava says it was worshipped, but it was a novelty, as Rabbi Abba bar Kahana listed eight things permitted that night.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah's question is cited: what is an animal set aside (מוקצה) for idolatry.
Resh Lakish defines that only an animal set aside for seven years is forbidden as מוקצה (set aside for idolatry).
Resh Lakish cites the verse about Gideon's bull, which was set aside for seven years, as the source for the seven-year threshold.
The Gemara objects: was that bull only מוקצה (set aside) and not also נעבד (worshipped)?
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the bull was set aside for worship but was not actually worshipped.
Rava answers that the bull was indeed worshipped, but it was a novelty (חידוש) permitted that night.
Rava supports his answer by citing Rabbi Abba bar Kahana's list of eight things permitted on that night, including the worship of the bull.

items.text: Opening Mishnah listing forbidden items
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah listing forbidden items
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are forbidden for the altar, including a vessel of service, an asherah, wood of an asherah, מוקצה, and נעבד.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items forbidden for the altar: a vessel of service, an asherah, wood of an asherah, מוקצה (set aside for idolatry), and נעבד (worshipped object).

items.text: Source for מוקצה from the Torah
items.text_en: Source for מוקצה from the Torah
items.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Mattana quotes Rabbi Yoshiya that the prohibition of מוקצה is derived from the verse 'תשמרו להקריב לי במועדו', implying that anything set aside for another master is forbidden. Abaye challenges this, but Rav Tovi explains that the verse refers to idolatry.

sub.text: Rav Tovi bar Masna citing Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.text_en: Rav Tovi bar Masna citing Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiya derives the prohibition of מוקצה (set aside for idolatry) from the verse 'תִּשְׁמְרוּ לְהַקְרִיב לִי בְּמוֹעֲדוֹ' — anything that is guarded for idolatry is excluded.
Abaye objects: if the criterion is guarding, then a lamb set aside for a fast day (not guarded for idolatry) would also be unfit for the altar, which is absurd.
Rav Tovi bar Masna clarifies: the verse says 'לִי' (to Me) and not to another master, specifically idolatry, so only guarding for idolatry disqualifies.

items.text: Dispute on when מוקצה becomes forbidden
items.text_en: Dispute on when מוקצה becomes forbidden
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Adda quotes Rav Yitzchak that מוקצה is forbidden only after it is worked with. Ulla quotes Rabbi Yochanan that it is forbidden only after it is handed over to idolatrous priests. Rabbi Yochanan adds that it is forbidden after it is fed idolatrous carshina (a type of feed). Rabbi Abba questions whether they disagree with Ulla, but is told that Ulla also refers to feeding carshina.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Adda quoting Rav Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Adda quoting Rav Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Adda quotes Rav Yitzchak that מוקצה (an animal set aside for idolatry) is forbidden only after it has been worked with.
Ulla quotes Rabbi Yochanan that מוקצה is forbidden only after it is handed over to idolatrous priests.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that מוקצה is forbidden only after it is fed carshina (a type of feed) of idolatry.
Rabbi Abba asks whether the two statements about feeding carshina contradict Ulla's earlier statement about handing over to priests.
The response clarifies that Ulla also refers to the act of feeding carshina, so there is no disagreement.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's praise and a baraita defining 'ma'aseh'
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's praise and a baraita defining 'ma'aseh'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba praises the ability to resolve the dispute, attributing it to his time in Eretz Yisrael. Rav Yitzchak says he was already knowledgeable. A baraita taught by Rav Chananya Tritaa before Rabbi Yochanan states that מוקצה is forbidden only after an action is performed, and Rabbi Yochanan explains that action means shearing and working with it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba praises his ability to resolve the dispute, attributing it to his time in Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Yitzchak objects that Rabbi Abba was already knowledgeable before going to Eretz Yisrael.

sub.text: Baraita taught by Rav Chananya Tritaa before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Baraita taught by Rav Chananya Tritaa before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: A baraita taught by Rav Chananya Tritaa before Rabbi Yochanan states that מוקצה (set-aside for idolatry) is forbidden only after an action is performed, and Rabbi Yochanan explains that action means shearing and working with it.

items.text: Source for נעבד and the case of a tereifah
items.text_en: Source for נעבד and the case of a tereifah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition of נעבד (an animal worshipped). Rav Pappa derives it from the verse 'ממשקה ישראל', meaning only what is permitted to Israel may be offered. The Gemara questions whether a tereifah, which is forbidden to common use, also needs a verse, and brings a baraita excluding tereifah from the altar. It then discusses cases where the tereifah was sanctified before or after becoming tereifah, and whether a verse is needed for a tereifah that had a moment of fitness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the prohibition of a נעבד (an animal worshipped).

Rav Pappa derives the prohibition from the verse 'ממשקה ישראל' (from what is permitted to Israel), arguing that if the animal were already forbidden to common use, no verse would be needed to exclude it from the altar.
The Gemara objects: is it true that wherever an animal is forbidden to common use no verse is needed? A tereifah is forbidden to common use, yet a verse excludes it from the altar.
A baraita is cited: the verse 'מן הבקר' (from the cattle) is superfluous and comes to exclude a tereifah from the altar.

The Gemara resolves: the verse for a tereifah is necessary, because one might think it applies only when the animal became a tereifah before sanctification, but if sanctified first and then became a tereifah, it might be permitted for the altar.
The Gemara objects: but the exclusion of a tereifah is already derived from the verse 'כל אשר יעבור תחת השבט' (all that passes under the rod), excluding a tereifah that cannot pass.

The Gemara resolves: that verse is also necessary, because one might think it applies only to a tereifah that never had a moment of fitness (born a tereifah), but if it had a moment of fitness and then became a tereifah, it might be permitted for the altar — so the verse teaches otherwise.

items.text: Mishnah on אתנן
items.text_en: Mishnah on אתנן
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines אתנן: if one says to a harlot 'Take this lamb as your hire', even if there are a hundred, all are forbidden. Similarly, if one says to another 'Take this lamb and let your maidservant sleep with my slave', Rabbi Meir says it is not אתנן, but the Sages say it is.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines אתנן (hire of a harlot) and presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding a case where one says 'take this lamb and have your maidservant sleep with my slave'.

The Mishnah presents a second case: one says to another 'Take this lamb and let your maidservant sleep with my slave,' and records the dispute between Rabbi Meir (who says it is not אתנן) and the Sages (who say it is).

items.text: Gemara on אתנן: case of multiple animals and timing
items.text_en: Gemara on אתנן: case of multiple animals and timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's case of a hundred animals is where she received one as hire and he gave a hundred, all are forbidden because they come from the power of the hire. A baraita discusses cases where payment was given before or after intercourse, and Rabbi Elazar questions whether the prohibition applies retroactively.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's case of a hundred animals all being forbidden is possible, since if she received a hundred animals as hire it would be obvious.
The Gemara answers that the case is where she received one animal as hire and he gave her a hundred, all forbidden because they come from the power of the hire.
A baraita is cited that initially states if he gave payment without intercourse or had intercourse without payment the אתנן (hire of a harlot) is permitted, but the Gemara objects to the wording.
The baraita is corrected to say: if he gave payment before intercourse or after intercourse, the אתנן (hire) is permitted.
Rabbi Elazar questions whether the prohibition of אתנן (hire) should apply retroactively to payment given before intercourse.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous Tanna of the Mishnah as Rabbi Elazar, who holds that a man who has intercourse with an unmarried woman not for the sake of marriage makes her a zonah. The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies an almanah (widow) rather than a penuyah (unmarried woman), and explains that the case of an almanah is necessary because one might think that since she is a biblical precedent, she should not be forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous Tanna of the Mishnah as Rabbi Elazar, who holds that a man who has intercourse with an unmarried woman not for the sake of marriage makes her a zonah.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies an almanah (widow) rather than a penuyah (unmarried woman), since Rabbi Elazar's principle would apply to any unmarried woman.

The Gemara explains that the case of an almanah is necessary because one might think that since she is a biblical precedent (בנין אב), she should not be forbidden, so the Mishnah teaches that she is indeed forbidden.

items.text: Dispute about the slave in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Dispute about the slave in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a shifchah (Canaanite maidservant) can be forbidden to a slave, since she is permitted to him. Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah refers to the slave's own slave (i.e., a Hebrew slave), but uses the term 'eved' loosely. Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak argues that it refers to a Hebrew slave, and the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis is about whether the Hebrew slave has a wife and children, which determines if his master can give him a Canaanite maidservant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a Canaanite maidservant (שפחה) is permitted to a slave (עבד), so how can the Mishnah forbid it?
Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah refers to the slave's own slave (a Hebrew slave), and the term 'עבד' is used loosely as a euphemism.
The Gemara asks: if so, what is Rabbi's reasoning for forbidding the maidservant?
Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak argues that the Mishnah actually refers to a Hebrew slave (עבד עברי), not a Canaanite slave.
The Gemara asks: if so, what is the Rabbis' reasoning, since a Canaanite maidservant is permitted to a Hebrew slave?
The Gemara resolves that the dispute is about a Hebrew slave who has no wife and children; the Rabbis hold that his master may not give him a Canaanite maidservant, while Rabbi holds that he may.

items.text: Mishnah: Definitions of mechir kelev and etnan zonah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definitions of mechir kelev and etnan zonah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines 'mechir kelev' as when one says to another 'Take this lamb in exchange for a dog.' It also discusses a case of partners dividing property, where one takes ten items and the other nine plus a dog; the items opposite the dog are forbidden, but those with the dog are permitted. Finally, it states that the etnan of a dog and the mechir of a zonah are permitted, as the verse says 'both of them' (shneihem) and not four, and their offspring are permitted as the verse says 'them' (hen) and not their offspring.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by defining 'mechir kelev' as when one says to another 'Take this lamb in exchange for a dog.'
The Mishnah provides a case of partners dividing property: one takes ten items and the other nine plus a dog; items opposite the dog are forbidden, but those with the dog are permitted.

The Mishnah concludes that the etnan of a dog and the mechir of a zonah are permitted, as the verse says 'both of them' (שְׁנֵיהֶם) and not four, and their offspring are permitted as the verse says 'them' (הֵן) and not their offspring.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving the exclusion of etnan and mechir
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving the exclusion of etnan and mechir
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa that defines 'mechir kelev' as the exchange for a dog. It then questions whether the verse could be read as referring to an actual etnan (of a zonah) and an actual mechir (of a dog), but notes that would make three items, while the verse says 'both of them' (shneihem), implying only two. The Gemara clarifies that the verse means etnan but not mechir, and mechir but not etnan, and proves this from the wording of the verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa defines 'mechir kelev' as the exchange for a dog, citing a verse from Psalms.

The Gemara questions whether the verse could refer to an actual etnan (of a zonah) and an actual mechir (of a dog), but notes that would make three items while the verse says 'both of them' (shneihem), implying only two.
The Gemara clarifies that the verse means etnan but not mechir, and mechir but not etnan, not both together.
The Gemara proves from the verse's wording that it refers to etnan of a zonah and mechir of a dog, not etnan of a dog or mechir of a zonah.

items.text: Clarifying the case of partners dividing property
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of partners dividing property
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why in the case of partners dividing property, the items opposite the dog are forbidden; one should take the dog against one item and the rest should be permitted. It answers that we are dealing with a case where the value of the dog exceeds one of the items, and that excess value is spread over all the items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why in the case of partners dividing property, the items opposite the dog are forbidden; one should take the dog against one item and the rest should be permitted.
The Gemara answers that we are dealing with a case where the value of the dog exceeds one of the items, and that excess value is spread over all the items.

items.text: Introduction of a new question
items.text_en: Introduction of a new question
items.desc_en: Rava of Parzakya asks Rav Ashi a question, beginning a new discussion about the Mishnah's ruling that etnan of a dog and mechir of a zonah are permitted.

sub.text: Rava of Parzakya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rava of Parzakya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rava of Parzakya asks Rav Ashi a question, initiating a new discussion about the Mishnah's ruling that etnan of a dog and mechir of a zonah are permitted.

items.text: Source for the permissibility of the hire of a dog and the price of a harlot
items.text_en: Source for the permissibility of the hire of a dog and the price of a harlot
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the rabbinic statement that there is no bestiality for animals. It cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'both of them' that the offspring of such animals are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rabbinic statement that there is no bestiality for animals, and suggests that the verse could have written 'the hire of a harlot and a dog' to exclude the offspring.
A baraita is cited that derives from the verse 'both of them' that the offspring of such animals are permitted, using the word 'them' to exclude the offspring.

items.text: Rava's ruling on offspring of a violated or goring animal, and the dispute about a מוקצה or נעבד
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on offspring of a violated or goring animal, and the dispute about a מוקצה or נעבד
items.desc_en: Rava states that the offspring of an animal that was violated is forbidden if the mother and her offspring were both violated. Similarly for a goring animal. Then a dispute is presented regarding the offspring of an animal that was set aside for idolatry or worshipped: one opinion permits it, another forbids it.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that the offspring of an animal that was violated is forbidden if the mother and her offspring were both violated, and similarly for a goring animal.

sub.text: First opinion on מוקצה and נעבד
sub.text_en: First opinion on מוקצה and נעבד
sub.desc_en: One opinion permits the offspring of an animal set aside for idolatry or worshipped, reasoning that the designation applies only to the mother.

sub.text: Second opinion on מוקצה and נעבד
sub.text_en: Second opinion on מוקצה and נעבד
sub.desc_en: Another opinion forbids the offspring, reasoning that the owner derives benefit from the offspring's existence.

items.text: Rav's ruling on consecrating with manure of a stoned ox or of idolatrous calves
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on consecrating with manure of a stoned ox or of idolatrous calves
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami quotes Rav: If one consecrates a woman with the manure of a stoned ox, she is consecrated; with the manure of idolatrous calves, she is not. Two reasons are given: a logical reason (one is pleased with the manure for idolatry but not for the ox) and a scriptural derivation.

sub.text: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami reports Rav's ruling: consecration with manure of a stoned ox is valid, but with manure of idolatrous calves is not, and then asks for the reason.
The Gemara offers a logical reason: one is pleased with the manure for idolatry but not for the stoned ox.
The Gemara offers a scriptural derivation: for idolatry the verse 'והיית חרם כמוהו' includes manure, while for the stoned ox the verse 'לא יאכל את בשרו' excludes manure.

items.text: Mishnah: Items given as payment to a harlot or for a dog
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items given as payment to a harlot or for a dog
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists what is permitted or forbidden when given as payment: money is permitted; items that can be offered on the altar are forbidden; consecrated items are permitted. Birds are forbidden, derived from the verse 'for any vow'. The Mishnah then discusses offspring of animals forbidden to the altar, with Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus adding their opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that money given as payment to a harlot is permitted.
The Mishnah lists items that can be offered on the altar as forbidden when given as payment.
The Mishnah states that consecrated items given as payment are permitted.
The Mishnah rules that birds are forbidden, derived from the verse 'for any vow'.
The Mishnah states that offspring of animals forbidden to the altar are permitted.
Rabbi Eliezer adds that the offspring of a טריפה (torn animal) may not be offered on the altar.
Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus adds that a kosher animal that nursed from a טריפה is disqualified from the altar.
The Mishnah concludes that consecrated animals that become טריפה may not be redeemed to feed to dogs.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on changed items
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on changed items
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: if a woman received wheat and made it into fine flour, etc., one source says forbidden, another says permitted. Rav Yosef identifies this as a dispute between Beit Shammai (forbid) and Beit Hillel (permit). Beit Hillel derives from 'them' that their offspring and their changes are excluded; Beit Shammai includes changes via 'also'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: one source says changed items are forbidden, another says they are permitted.
Rav Yosef identifies the dispute as between Beit Shammai (forbid) and Beit Hillel (permit).
The Gemara explains that Beit Hillel derives exclusion of changes from 'them', while Beit Shammai includes changes via 'also', and raises a difficulty for Beit Hillel regarding the word 'also'.

items.text: Exegesis of 'the house of the Lord your God' regarding the red heifer and beaten plates
items.text_en: Exegesis of 'the house of the Lord your God' regarding the red heifer and beaten plates
items.desc_en: A baraita interprets the verse to exclude the red heifer (which does not enter the Temple), according to Rabbi Elazar. The Sages say it includes beaten plates. Rav Chisda identifies these Sages as Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who holds that even beaten plates for the back of the Ark-cover are not made from such gold.

sub.desc_en: A baraita interprets the verse 'בית ה' אלהיך' (the house of the Lord your God) to exclude the red heifer, which does not enter the Temple, according to Rabbi Elazar.
The Sages say the verse includes beaten plates (ריקועין) as subject to the prohibition.
Rav Chisda identifies the Sages as Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who holds that even beaten plates for the back of the Ark-cover are not made from such gold.

items.text: Gemara: Why consecrated items are not subject to the law of payment
items.text_en: Gemara: Why consecrated items are not subject to the law of payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why consecrated items are permitted, given a kal vachomer from birds. It answers that the verse 'for any vow' excludes vowed items. It then asks how consecrated items could be considered payment if they are not his property, and Rav Hoshaya explains the case is about one who appoints others on his Paschal lamb, following Rabbi's opinion that such money is considered non-sacred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if birds, which are not invalidated by a blemish, are subject to the law of payment (אתנן ומחיר), then consecrated items, which are invalidated by a blemish, should certainly be subject to it.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'for any vow' (לכל נדר) excludes vowed items (הנדור), i.e., consecrated items, from the law of payment.
The Gemara objects: if not for the verse, would we think payment applies to consecrated items? But they are not his property (לאו ממונא הוא) to give as payment.

Rav Hoshaya explains that the case involves one who appoints others on his Paschal lamb, following Rabbi's opinion that such money is considered non-sacred (חולין), because Israel consecrated their Paschal lambs on condition that they could appoint others.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding offspring of forbidden animals
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding offspring of forbidden animals
items.desc_en: Rav states that offspring of animals forbidden to the altar are permitted, but a baraita adds that Rabbi Eliezer forbids. Rav Nachman and Rava debate the parameters of the dispute: whether it concerns animals that became pregnant and then were violated, or violated and then became pregnant, or the status of the animals when violated (consecrated vs. non-consecrated). Two versions of the debate are presented.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that offspring of animals forbidden to the altar are permitted, but a baraita adds that Rabbi Eliezer forbids.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chinana citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the dispute applies when animals became pregnant and then were violated, based on whether a fetus is considered part of the mother; if violated first and then pregnant, all agree the offspring is permitted.
Rava argues that the dispute is when animals were violated and then became pregnant, based on whether a combined permitted and prohibited cause yields a permitted or prohibited result.

Rava concludes that if animals became pregnant and then were violated, all agree the offspring is prohibited, consistent with his own ruling that the offspring of a violated or goring pregnant animal is forbidden.

sub.text: Alternative version citing Rav Huna bar Chinana citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Alternative version citing Rav Huna bar Chinana citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that the dispute is when animals were violated while consecrated, based on whether this constitutes degradation; if violated while non-sacred, all agree the offspring is permitted.
Rava counters that the dispute is when animals were violated while non-sacred, based on degradation; if violated while consecrated, all agree the offspring is prohibited.

items.text: Dispute about the offspring of a terefah
items.text_en: Dispute about the offspring of a terefah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding the offspring of a terefah animal. It presents two scenarios based on differing views about whether a terefah can give birth or survive, linking the dispute to the principles of 'this and that cause' and 'the fetus is a limb of its mother'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah's dispute about the offspring of a terefah animal and presents the first scenario: the animal was made terefah and then became pregnant.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages dispute based on the principle of 'this and that cause' (זֶה וָזֶה גּוֹרֵם): Rabbi Eliezer forbids, the Sages permit.
The Gemara presents the second scenario: the animal became pregnant and then was made terefah, and the dispute is whether the fetus is considered a limb of its mother (עוּבָּר יֶרֶךְ אִמּוֹ).

items.text: Rav Huna's statement about the egg of a terefah bird and the ensuing debate
items.text_en: Rav Huna's statement about the egg of a terefah bird and the ensuing debate
items.desc_en: Rav Huna asserts that the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer that the egg of a terefah bird is forbidden, because it grows from the bird's body. Rava supports this with a baraita about maggots from a living person, but Abaye objects, arguing that the egg becomes permitted once it rots, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer concedes the egg is permitted. Rava accepts the baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer that the chick of a terefah egg is forbidden, because the egg grows from the hen's body itself.
Rava cites a baraita about a spoonful of maggots from a living person, where the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer only regarding the egg, not the maggots.
Abaye objects, arguing the opposite: the Sages disagree with Rabbi Eliezer only about maggots, because a living person is called 'maggot' in Scripture.

Abaye argues that regarding the egg, it only grows when it rots and becomes mere dust, so even Rabbi Eliezer would agree; he then cites a baraita that explicitly states Rabbi Eliezer agrees the chick is permitted, and Rav Huna concedes.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus's statement about a kosher animal that nursed from a terefah
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus's statement about a kosher animal that nursed from a terefah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus's ruling that a kosher animal that nursed from a terefah is permitted. It rejects the idea that it is forbidden due to being fattened by the terefah, and instead explains that it is permitted because the milk was hot and the animal could survive without it for a day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the reasoning of Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, who says a terefah animal that nursed from a kosher animal is permitted, and rejects the idea that it is because it was fattened by the kosher animal.
Rabbi Chanina Tritaita teaches before Rabbi Yochanan that the case is where the terefah animal nursed scalding milk from morning to morning, because it can survive on that for a full day.

items.text: The source for not redeeming consecrated animals that become terefah
items.text_en: The source for not redeeming consecrated animals that become terefah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita deriving from the verse 'תִּזְבַּח וְאָכַלְתָּ' that consecrated animals which become terefah cannot be redeemed to feed to dogs. An alternative version holds that the verse teaches that permission to eat only begins after slaughter, implying that one may redeem them to feed to dogs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that consecrated animals that become terefah cannot be redeemed to feed to dogs, and cites a baraita deriving it from the verse 'תִּזְבַּח וְאָכַלְתָּ' (you shall slaughter and eat).
An alternative version holds that the verse permits eating only from the time of slaughter onward, implying that one may redeem consecrated animals to feed to dogs.
An alternative version holds that the verse teaches that permission to eat begins only after slaughter, implying that one may redeem them to feed to dogs.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter and beginning of the next Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter and beginning of the next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The chapter concludes with 'הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ' and the next Mishnah begins, listing differences between קָדְשֵׁי מִזְבֵּחַ and קָדְשֵׁי בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת, such as the laws of temurah, piggul, notar, and tumah.

sub.desc_en: The chapter concludes with the formula 'הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ' (we return to you).
The Mishnah begins by stating that there are differences between קָדְשֵׁי מִזְבֵּחַ (altar sanctities) and קָדְשֵׁי בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת (Temple maintenance sanctities).
The Mishnah lists that קָדְשֵׁי מִזְבֵּחַ (altar sanctities) are subject to temurah, piggul, notar, and tumah, unlike קָדְשֵׁי בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת (Temple maintenance sanctities).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists differences between Kodshei Mizbe'ach and Kodshei Bedek HaBayit: for Kodshei Mizbe'ach, offspring and milk are forbidden after redemption, slaughtering them outside is liable, and they are not given to craftsmen as payment, unlike Kodshei Bedek HaBayit. For Kodshei Bedek HaBayit, unspecified dedications go to the Temple treasury, sanctity applies to everything, me'ilah applies to their growth, and the owners have no benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the first set of differences between Kodshei Mizbe'ach and Kodshei Bedek HaBayit: for Kodshei Mizbe'ach, offspring and milk are forbidden after redemption, slaughtering them outside is liable, and they are not given to craftsmen as payment.

The Mishnah lists the second set of differences: for Kodshei Bedek HaBayit, unspecified dedications go to the Temple treasury, sanctity applies to everything, me'ilah applies to their growth, and the owners have no benefit.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Are all Kodshei Mizbe'ach subject to temurah?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Are all Kodshei Mizbe'ach subject to temurah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's blanket statement that all Kodshei Mizbe'ach are subject to temurah, citing exceptions: birds and meal-offerings do not effect temurah, and a firstborn does not effect temurah. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers only to animals, and that the case of a firstborn follows Rabbi Yehuda's view. It further clarifies that the Mishnah's rule applies to the original animal, not to temurah itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's implication that all Kodshei Mizbe'ach can undergo temurah, citing that birds and meal-offerings cannot.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's rule applies only to animal offerings, not birds or meal-offerings.
The Gemara objects that the offspring of a consecrated animal is itself Kodshei Mizbe'ach, yet a baraita states it cannot undergo temurah.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that an offspring can undergo temurah.
The Gemara objects that a temurah animal itself is Kodshei Mizbe'ach, yet a baraita states it cannot undergo temurah.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's rule applies only to the original animal, not to a temurah.
The Gemara concludes that even according to the Rabbis, the Mishnah's rule applies only to the original animal, not to offspring or temurah.

items.text: Gemara on giving to craftsmen
items.text_en: Gemara on giving to craftsmen
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Kodshei Mizbe'ach are not given to craftsmen as payment, implying that Kodshei Bedek HaBayit may be given. Rabbi Avahu answers with a verse: 'And they shall make for Me' – from what is Mine, meaning that items dedicated to the Temple may be used for payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Kodshei Bedek HaBayit may be given to craftsmen as payment.
Rabbi Avahu answers that the verse 'וְעָשׂוּ לִי' (they shall make for Me) implies using only what is already dedicated to God, not paying craftsmen with consecrated items.

items.text: Dispute about unspecified dedications and the Tanna's identity
items.text_en: Dispute about unspecified dedications and the Tanna's identity
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tanna of the Mishnah's statement that unspecified dedications go to Bedek HaBayit as not Rabbi Yehoshua. It cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua argue about dedicating property containing animals fit for the altar: Rabbi Eliezer says males are sold for olot and females for shelamim, with proceeds to Bedek HaBayit; Rabbi Yehoshua says males themselves are offered as olot. Rav Adda bar Ahava explains their dispute depends on whether the herd is all males or mixed, and whether there are other assets. Two versions of Rav's statement are given, and the Gemara reconciles the wording of the baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's rule that unspecified dedications go to Bedek HaBayit and asks who the Tanna is.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that the Mishnah's Tanna is not Rabbi Yehoshua.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute the fate of animals in dedicated property: Rabbi Eliezer says males are sold for olot and females for shelamim, with proceeds to Bedek HaBayit; Rabbi Yehoshua says males themselves are offered as olot.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava reports Rav's first version: in a herd of all males, even Rabbi Eliezer agrees that the animals go to the altar, as no one would abandon קדשי מזבח (altar-dedicated items) for Bedek HaBayit.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava in the name of Rav (continued)
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava in the name of Rav (continued)
sub.desc_en: Rav explains that the dispute is only in a mixed herd: Rabbi Eliezer holds that one does not split his vow, so since females cannot be olot, males also go to Bedek HaBayit; Rabbi Yehoshua holds that one can split his vow.
An alternative version of Rav's statement: if only animals were dedicated (no other assets), even Rabbi Eliezer agrees they go to the altar.

The alternative version says the dispute is only when there are other assets: Rabbi Eliezer holds one does not split his vow, so animals go to Bedek HaBayit; Rabbi Yehoshua holds one can split his vow.
The Gemara reconciles the baraita's wording 'with other assets' with the first version, noting that a supporting baraita reads 'their proceeds fall to Bedek HaBayit' without mentioning other assets.

items.text: Clarifying 'sanctity applies to everything' and 'me'ilah in growth'
items.text_en: Clarifying 'sanctity applies to everything' and 'me'ilah in growth'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'sanctity applies to everything' includes improvements and offshoots (shippuyei veniva). Regarding 'me'ilah in growth', Rav Pappa says it includes milk of consecrated animals and eggs of doves in the sanctity of the altar, citing a baraita that distinguishes between Kodshei Mizbe'ach and Kodshei Bedek HaBayit. Even according to the view that me'ilah applies to growth of Mizbe'ach, this is only for growth fit for the altar, not for unfit growth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional items are included by the statement that sanctity of Bedek HaBayit applies to everything.
Ravina answers that it includes improvements and offshoots (shippuyei veniva).
The Gemara asks what additional items are included by the rule that one commits me'ilah in the growth of consecrated property.
Rav Pappa answers that it includes, in the sanctity of the altar, the milk of consecrated animals and the eggs of doves.
A baraita is cited that distinguishes between Kodshei Mizbe'ach, where milk and eggs are prohibited but not subject to me'ilah, and Kodshei Bedek HaBayit, where me'ilah does apply.
The Gemara resolves that even according to the view that me'ilah applies to growth of Mizbe'ach, this is only for growth fit for the altar, not for unfit growth.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that neither sacrifices for the altar nor items for Temple upkeep may be transferred from one sanctity to another, but they may be dedicated for a higher purpose or declared herem; if they die, they are buried. Rabbi Shimon adds that items for Temple upkeep may be redeemed if they die.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that neither altar sacrifices nor Temple upkeep items may be transferred to a different sanctity, but they may be dedicated for a higher purpose or declared herem; if they die, they are buried.
Rabbi Shimon adds that Temple upkeep items, if they die, may be redeemed.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one transfers sanctity from altar sacrifices to priestly herem, it is void, citing a verse that all herem is most holy to God.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that transferring sanctity from altar sacrifices to priestly herem is void.
Rav Huna cites the verse 'כל חרם קדש קדשים הוא לה׳' to prove that any herem from sacred items belongs to God.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that if one transfers items of Temple upkeep to altar sacrifices or priestly herem, it is void; similarly, if one transfers priestly herem to altar sacrifices or Temple upkeep, it is void. The implication is that transferring altar sacrifices to priestly herem is effective, posing a contradiction to Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that transferring items of Temple upkeep (בדק הבית) to either altar sacrifices or priestly herem is void.
The baraita continues: transferring priestly herem to either altar sacrifices or Temple upkeep is also void.
The gemara infers from the baraita's omission that transferring altar sacrifices to priestly herem is effective, posing a contradiction (תיוובתא) to Rav Huna's ruling.

items.text: Rav Huna's defense
items.text_en: Rav Huna's defense
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that the baraita only permits transferring altar sacrifices to Temple upkeep, not to priestly herem. The Gemara questions why the baraita did not include this case, and answers that the tanna only includes cases with two possibilities, not one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna defends his position by explaining that the baraita's exception (שייר) applies only to the case of consecrating altar sacrifices for Temple upkeep (בדק הבית), not for priestly herem (חרמי כהנים).
The Gemara asks why the baraita did not explicitly include the case of altar sacrifices to priestly herem among its listed exceptions.
The Gemara answers that the tanna only includes cases with two possible outcomes (תרתי), not cases with only one outcome.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah
