items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from the Mishnah's phrase 'dedicate them for a higher purpose' and 'declare them herem', suggesting that 'higher purpose' means Temple upkeep and 'herem' means priestly herem. The Gemara deflects by saying both terms refer to Temple upkeep.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from the Mishnah, suggesting that 'higher purpose' means Temple upkeep and 'herem' means priestly herem.
The Gemara deflects by saying both terms refer to Temple upkeep.

items.text: Refutation from a baraita
items.text_en: Refutation from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states that 'higher purpose' means Temple upkeep and 'herem' means priestly herem, and that transferring altar sacrifices to priestly herem is effective. This is a conclusive refutation of Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a baraita explicitly defines 'higher purpose' as Temple upkeep and 'herem' as priestly herem, contradicting the earlier interpretation.
A second baraita is cited, stating that transferring altar sacrifices to priestly herem is effective, directly refuting Rav Huna.
The Gemara concludes that this is a conclusive refutation of Rav Huna's opinion.

items.text: Ulla's alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Ulla's alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Huna cited a verse, and Ulla explains the verse differently: 'herem of all herem' indicates that only herem from something already most holy is for God. The Gemara then questions Ulla's consistency with another statement about transferring an olah to Temple upkeep.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Huna's ruling is based on a verse, so how can it be refuted?
Ulla explains that the verse 'חרם כל חרם' (a herem of all herem) means only a herem from something already most holy is for God, not a herem from ordinary consecrated items.
The Gemara questions whether Ulla's interpretation is consistent with his own statement elsewhere.

The Gemara cites Ulla's own ruling that one who transfers an עולה (burnt offering) to Temple upkeep (בדק הבית) only creates a delay (עיכוב), implying the transfer is effective, contradicting his current position.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the need for a verse for מעילה in חרמים
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the need for a verse for מעילה in חרמים
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse is needed to include חרמים in the law of מעילה, given that they are already called קדשי קדשים. It resolves by analogy to the case of קדשים קלים, where a verse is also needed despite being called קדשי קדשים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the only restriction on consecrating an עולה (burnt offering) to בדק הבית (Temple maintenance) is the prohibition of גזברין (treasurers) from using it.
The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition is rabbinic (מדרבנן), and the verse comes to teach the law of מעילה (misuse of consecrated property).
The Gemara questions why a verse is needed for מעילה (misuse) regarding חרמים (dedicated items), since they are already called קדשי קדשים (most holy things).
Rabbi Yannai states that explicit מעילה (misuse) from the Torah is only for עולה (burnt offering), while חטאת (sin offering) and אשם (guilt offering) are derived from Rabbi's teaching.

A baraita cites Rabbi who derives from the verse 'כל חלב לה׳' (all fat to the Lord) that the אמורים (sacrificial portions) of קדשים קלים (lesser holy things) are included in the law of מעילה (misuse).
The Gemara resolves that just as קדשים קלים (lesser holy things) need a verse for מעילה (misuse) despite being called קדשי קדשים (most holy things), so too חרמים (dedicated items) need a verse.

items.text: Discussion of the mishnah's ruling on an עולה dedicated to בדק הבית
items.text_en: Discussion of the mishnah's ruling on an עולה dedicated to בדק הבית
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the mishnah's statement that such an animal is only subject to the prohibition of גזברין, citing a baraita that forbids slaughter until redemption. It resolves that the prohibition is rabbinic, and explains the phrase 'two מעילות' as referring to potential liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah's ruling that an עולה dedicated to בדק הבית is only subject to the prohibition of גזברין.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that forbids slaughtering such an animal until it is redeemed.
The Gemara answers that the prohibition is only rabbinic (מדרבנן), as supported by the baraita's continuation that if one violated and slaughtered, the act is valid.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the first answer
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the first answer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the prohibition is only rabbinic, why does the baraita mention 'two מעילות' (acts of misuse)?
The Gemara resolves that the phrase 'two מעילות' refers to potential liability, not actual liability.

items.text: Continuation of the mishnah: 'If they died, they shall be buried'
items.text_en: Continuation of the mishnah: 'If they died, they shall be buried'
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if animals consecrated for the Temple treasury die, they are buried, implying they cannot be redeemed. This sets up the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that if animals consecrated for the Temple treasury die, they are buried, implying they cannot be redeemed.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding העמדה והערכה
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding העמדה והערכה
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds that both קדשי מזבח and קדשי בדק הבית require העמדה והערכה according to the Rabbis. Reish Lakish limits this to קדשי בדק הבית only. Both agree that according to Rabbi Shimon, קדשי בדק הבית do not require it, while קדשי מזבח do, and that a blemished animal from the start never requires it.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yochanan from the mishnah and Reish Lakish's response
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yochanan from the mishnah and Reish Lakish's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah's explicit mention of 'קדשי בדק הבית' supports Rabbi Yochanan, as it would be unnecessary according to Reish Lakish. Reish Lakish explains that Rabbi Shimon was clarifying his position to the Tanna Kamma, who thought he disagreed on all consecrated animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah where Rabbi Shimon explicitly mentions 'קדשי בדק הבית' (consecrated property of the Temple treasury), arguing that this supports Rabbi Yochanan's position that both types of consecrated animals require evaluation.

The Gemara challenges Reish Lakish: if Rabbi Shimon only disagreed regarding קדשי בדק הבית (consecrated property of the Temple treasury), why did he need to specify 'קדשי בדק הבית' — he could have simply said 'if they die, they shall be redeemed'.

Reish Lakish explains that Rabbi Shimon did not know what the Tanna Kamma meant, so he clarified: 'I agree with you regarding קדשי מזבח (consecrated animals for the altar), but regarding קדשי בדק הבית (consecrated property of the Temple treasury) — if they die, they shall be redeemed.'

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that interprets the verse 'אם בהמה אשר יקריבו ממנה' as referring to blemished animals that require redemption, supporting Rabbi Yochanan's view that all consecrated animals require העמדה והערכה.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that interprets the verse 'אם בהמה אשר יקריבו ממנה' as referring to blemished animals that require redemption, supporting Rabbi Yochanan's view that all consecrated animals require העמדה והערכה.

items.text: Scriptural derivation for the requirement of standing and valuation
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation for the requirement of standing and valuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the biblical source that animals with a permanent blemish require standing and valuation before redemption, excluding those with a temporary blemish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the biblical source for requiring standing and valuation for animals with a permanent blemish, excluding those with a temporary blemish.
The Gemara concludes that the Torah commands standing and valuation for such animals.

items.text: Resh Lakish's position on קדשי בדק הבית
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's position on קדשי בדק הבית
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel cites Rav to explain Resh Lakish's view that only קדשי בדק הבית are subject to standing and valuation, based on the verse 'בין טוב ובין רע' and the exclusion of קדשי מזבח by 'אותה'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav asks for the reasoning of Reish Lakish, who holds that Temple-maintenance sanctities require standing and valuation but altar sanctities do not.
Rav explains that the verse uses 'אותה' (it) to exclude altar sanctities from the requirement.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's position and the challenge from Levi's baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's position and the challenge from Levi's baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'אותה' to exclude an animal blemished from birth. The baraita of Levi's school, which includes even such animals in standing and valuation, poses a difficulty for this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yochanan excludes with the word 'אותה' (it), and answers that he excludes an animal blemished from birth.
The Gemara objects that the baraita of Levi's school includes even an animal blemished from birth in standing and valuation, posing a difficulty for Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of 'אותה'.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's position and a difficulty
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's position and a difficulty
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Rav to explain Rabbi Shimon's view that קדשי מזבח are subject to standing and valuation, excluding קדשי בדק הבית. The Gemara raises a difficulty: the verse 'בין טוב ובין רע' should be superfluous.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in Rav's name explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: the verse 'בין טוב ובין רע' applies to items that vary in quality (קדשי מזבח), and 'אותה' excludes קדשי בדק הבית.
The Gemara objects: if the verse is used to distinguish between good and bad, then the phrase 'בין טוב ובין רע' itself should be superfluous, posing a difficulty.

items.text: First baraita as a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: First baraita as a challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A baraita states that for קדשי מזבח, blemished animals are redeemed, while for קדשי בדק הבית, all are buried. Rabbi Shimon disagrees. This appears to refute Rabbi Yochanan, but he explains it deals with animals blemished from birth, which is supported by the fact that Rabbi Shimon does not dispute the first clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a baraita as a challenge: for קדשי מזבח (altar sanctities), perfect animals are buried and blemished ones are redeemed, while for קדשי בדק הבית (Temple treasury sanctities), all are buried.
Rabbi Shimon disagrees, stating that for both types of sanctities, perfect animals are buried and blemished ones are redeemed.
The Gemara declares that this baraita is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan from its first clause.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that the baraita deals with animals that were blemished from birth (בעל מום מעיקרו), not those that became blemished after consecration.

The Gemara provides support for Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation: if the baraita dealt with animals whose blemish came after consecration, Rabbi Shimon would have disputed the first clause, so it must be about animals blemished from birth.

items.text: Second baraita and resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Second baraita and resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: A second baraita reverses the rulings, challenging Resh Lakish. Resh Lakish explains it deals with animals blemished after consecration, and that Rabbi Shimon indeed disputes it. Rabbi Yirmeya questions Resh Lakish's consistency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Resh Lakish by citing a baraita that contradicts his position.
Resh Lakish explains the baraita deals with animals blemished after consecration, but the Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon should then dispute it.
Resh Lakish reverses the baraita and cites another version that supports his view, challenging Rabbi Yochanan.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that the baraita deals with animals blemished from the outset, and the Gemara notes the consistency.
The Gemara again challenges Resh Lakish with the baraita.
Resh Lakish explains the baraita deals with animals blemished after consecration, and that Rabbi Shimon indeed disputes it.
Rabbi Yirmeya questions Resh Lakish's consistency regarding consecrated animals for the altar.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that blemished animals are redeemed, suggesting it implies that consecrated animals can be redeemed to feed to dogs, which is problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that blemished animals are redeemed, suggesting it implies that consecrated animals can be redeemed to feed to dogs, which is problematic.

items.text: Resolution: the case of animals slaughtered after blemish
items.text_en: Resolution: the case of animals slaughtered after blemish
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah deals with animals that were slaughtered after becoming blemished, citing a Tosefta where Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute whether such animals are buried or redeemed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: With what case are we dealing here?
The Gemara answers: It deals with animals that were slaughtered after becoming blemished.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir says such animals are buried, and the Sages say they are redeemed.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira about Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira about Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira why, according to Rabbi Shimon who exempts Temple treasury consecrations from standing and valuation, unblemished animals should be buried; the answer is that they are fit for sacrifice, as per a baraita.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira why, according to Rabbi Shimon who exempts Temple treasury consecrations from standing and valuation, unblemished animals should be buried.
The Gemara answers that they are fit for sacrifice, as per a baraita stating that animals designated for the Temple treasury, when redeemed, are only redeemed for the altar.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye about Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question to Abaye about Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rava) questions Rabbi Yochanan's view that the Mishnah deals with a permanent blemish from the outset, and challenges whether everyone agrees that such an animal is not subject to standing and valuation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or Rava) challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position that the Mishnah deals with a permanent blemish from the outset, questioning whether everyone agrees that such an animal is not subject to standing and valuation.

items.text: Proof from a Mishnah and Rav Yehuda's attribution to Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Proof from a Mishnah and Rav Yehuda's attribution to Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about animals with a prior blemish that are redeemed, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that this is the view of Rabbi Shimon, who distinguishes between altar and Temple treasury consecrations, and that Rabbi Shimon agrees that a permanent blemish from the outset is redeemed, while the Sages disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about animals with a prior permanent blemish that are redeemed and become ordinary property.
The baraita continues listing the halachic status of such animals after redemption.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Shimon, who distinguishes between altar and Temple treasury consecrations.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon agrees a permanent blemish from the outset is redeemed, while the Sages disagree and include it in the requirement of standing and valuation.

items.text: Clarification of the identity of the Sages and Rav's position
items.text_en: Clarification of the identity of the Sages and Rav's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions who the Sages are, identifying them as the school of Levi, and then discusses why Rav's statement only says 'this is the view of Rabbi Shimon' without mentioning the dispute, offering two explanations: either Rav follows Resh Lakish's view that Temple treasury consecrations are subject to standing and valuation, or he follows Rabbi Yochanan and the text should read 'and his dispute'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the 'Sages' are in the earlier baraita.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Levi
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Levi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Sages are the Tanna of the school of Levi.
The Gemara objects that if so, Rav's statement should have said 'this is the view of Rabbi Shimon and his dispute' rather than just 'this is the view of Rabbi Shimon'.
The Gemara answers that Rav follows Resh Lakish's view that Temple treasury consecrations are subject to standing and valuation, so the dispute is only about altar consecrations.
The Gemara notes that the baraita's opening and closing clauses (if they die they are redeemed vs. buried) support this interpretation.
Alternatively, Rav follows Rabbi Yochanan, and the text should indeed read 'and his dispute'.

items.text: Mishnah: items that are buried or burned
items.text_en: Mishnah: items that are buried or burned
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are buried (e.g., animals that miscarried, the heifer whose neck is broken, etc.) and items that are burned (e.g., leaven on Passover, impure terumah, etc.), with a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages regarding non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens the list of items that are buried (נקברין), including sacred animals that miscarried, the placenta, the stoned ox, the heifer whose neck is broken, the birds of the metzora, and the hair of the nazirite.

The Mishnah continues the list of buried items, adding the firstborn donkey, meat in milk, and non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard, with Rabbi Shimon arguing that these should be burned (ישרפו) rather than buried.

The Mishnah lists items that are burned (נשרפין): leaven on Passover, impure תרומה (priestly portion), orlah fruit, diverse vineyard seeds, and all sacred animals slaughtered outside their proper time or place.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: rules for burning and burying doubtful offerings
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: rules for burning and burying doubtful offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a suspensive guilt-offering is burned, while Rabbi Yehuda says it is buried. A doubt-offering bird sin-offering is burned, but Rabbi Yehuda says to throw it into the channel. All buried items may not be burned, and all burned items may not be buried; Rabbi Yehuda permits one to be stringent and burn buried items, but the Sages forbid changing the practice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a suspensive guilt-offering (אשם תלוי) is burned, while Rabbi Yehuda says it is buried; a doubt-offering bird sin-offering (חטאת העוף הבאה על הספק) is burned, but Rabbi Yehuda says to throw it into the channel.

The Mishnah continues with a general rule: all buried items may not be burned, and all burned items may not be buried; Rabbi Yehuda permits one to be stringent and burn buried items, but the Sages forbid changing the practice.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction about nazirite hair and firstborn donkey wool
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction about nazirite hair and firstborn donkey wool
items.desc_en: Tavi raises a contradiction to Rav Nachman: the Mishnah says nazirite hair is buried, but a baraita says that weaving a sit's worth of firstborn wool into a garment requires burning the garment, and nazirite hair or firstborn donkey wool in a sack requires burning the sack. Rav Nachman distinguishes between a contaminated nazirite (buried) and a pure nazirite (burned). Tavi objects that the contradiction remains for nazirite vs. nazirite and firstborn donkey vs. firstborn donkey. Rav Sheshet resolves: one case is with a sack (burned), the other with hair (buried). Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Elazar offer similar distinctions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the Mishnah's rule that nazirite hair is buried.

Tavi raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says nazirite hair is buried, but a baraita says that weaving a sit's worth of firstborn wool into a garment requires burning the garment, and nazirite hair or firstborn donkey wool in a sack requires burning the sack.
Rav Nachman distinguishes: the Mishnah refers to a contaminated nazirite (buried), while the baraita refers to a pure nazirite (burned).
Tavi objects that the contradiction remains for nazirite vs. nazirite and firstborn donkey vs. firstborn donkey, and Rav Nachman is silent.
Rav Sheshet resolves: one case involves a sack (burned), the other involves hair (buried).

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Elazar's statements
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Elazar's statements
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Elazar offer similar distinctions: one case is a sack (burned), the other hair (buried); or one is a pure nazirite (burned), the other a contaminated nazirite (buried).

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding nullification and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding nullification and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: the sack should be nullified by the majority (רוב). Rav Pappa answers that the case involves a ציפורתא (a small amount). The questioner then asks why not simply remove the hairs. Rabbi Yirmeya suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who permits burning buried items. The questioner objects that the difficulty is about removing the hairs, not about burning. The Gemara clarifies: if possible, remove them; if not, the ruling aligns with Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The questioner objects that the sack should be nullified by the majority (רוב) of permitted wool.
Rav Pappa answers that the case involves a ציפורתא (a small amount of forbidden hair), which is not nullified.
The questioner asks why not simply remove the small amount of hairs from the sack.
Rabbi Yirmeya suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who permits burning buried items, so the sack is burned entirely.

items.text: List of burned items and Rabbi Yehuda's practice for bird sin-offering
items.text_en: List of burned items and Rabbi Yehuda's practice for bird sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are burned: leaven on Passover (the Tanna rules like Rabbi Yehuda that burning is the only removal), impure terumah and orlah (food burned, liquids buried). A baraita describes Rabbi Yehuda's practice for the doubt-offering bird sin-offering: he throws it into the channel, dismembers it limb by limb, and throws them into the channel, where it rolls down to the Kidron Valley.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are burned, beginning with leaven on Passover, and the Gemara notes that the Tanna rules like Rabbi Yehuda that burning is the only removal.
The Mishnah continues with impure terumah and orlah, specifying that food is burned and liquids are buried.

items.text: Reason for the distinction: ashes of buried vs. burned items
items.text_en: Reason for the distinction: ashes of buried vs. burned items
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's rule: buried items' ashes are forbidden, while burned items' ashes are permitted. It questions this: are buried items' ashes really forbidden? A baraita says blood of a menstruant and flesh of a corpse that crumble are pure, but that means pure and forbidden. Similarly, a bird olah's crop and feathers after blood manipulation are free from me'ilah but still forbidden. For burned sacred items, a baraita says all burned items' ashes are permitted except for an asherah's ashes, and consecrated ashes are always forbidden. The Gemara resolves that the baraita does not include consecrated ashes with asherah because asherah has nullification by a gentile, while consecrated items have no eternal nullification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the Mishnah's rule that buried items' ashes are forbidden while burned items' ashes are permitted.
The Gemara objects: a baraita states that crumbled blood of a menstruant and flesh of a corpse are pure, implying they are permitted, but the Gemara clarifies they are pure yet forbidden.
Rav Pinchas objects with a baraita about a bird olah: after blood manipulation, its crop and feathers are free from me'ilah but still forbidden, not permitted.

The Gemara objects further: a baraita says all burned items' ashes are permitted except for asherah ashes, and consecrated ashes are always forbidden, contradicting the Mishnah's claim that consecrated burned ashes are permitted.

The Gemara resolves: the baraita does not group consecrated ashes with asherah because asherah has nullification by a gentile, while consecrated items have no eternal nullification, so consecrated ashes are always forbidden.

items.text: Resolution: cases where consecrated ashes are permitted
items.text_en: Resolution: cases where consecrated ashes are permitted
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama suggests a case where a fire broke out on its own in consecrated wood, with no identifiable person to commit me'ilah, so the ashes may go to non-sacred use. Rav Shemayah says the baraita about consecrated ashes being always forbidden refers to the ashes of the daily removal (תרומת הדשן), which are always forbidden, as derived from the verse: 'and he shall place it' (וְשָׂמוֹ) — gently, entirely, without scattering.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama proposes a case where a fire broke out on its own in consecrated wood, with no identifiable person to commit me'ilah, so the ashes may go to non-sacred use.
Rav Shemayah counters that the baraita about consecrated ashes being always forbidden refers specifically to the ashes of the daily removal (תרומת הדשן), which are perpetually forbidden.
A baraita is cited deriving from the verse 'וְשָׂמוֹ' (and he shall place it) that the ashes must be placed gently, entirely, and without scattering, supporting the perpetual prohibition.
